tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

# Repository Access Service — Plan

Working doc. Update checkboxes as things get built. Keep entries short.

## Scoring reality check (from instructions)
25% tradeoff quality · 25% ambiguities surfaced · 25% code quality/typed contract ·
15% change-request absorption · 10% BENCH.md. **Feature completeness is not scored.**
So: a sharp README > a fuller feature set. Don't burn the 4h chasing frontend polish
if R1–R4 + README aren't solid.

Hard requirements regardless of scoring weight:
- `docker compose up` from clean clone, no manual steps, must work.
- R4 oracle is required, not optional, and must not share code with the fast path.
- Commit as you go (real messages) — they read history to verify change-request timing.
- `agent-transcripts/` raw logs — don't clean these up, don't skip messy ones.

## Chosen design (the R1/R2 tradeoff)
Point picked: **cache the resolved path, invalidate coarsely.**
- Cache key: `subject_id` → `{path: [user, team, team, ..., resource], role, created_at}`.
- Cache hit → check is O(1) dict lookup, and the stored path *is* the R3 explanation
  (this is why we don't cache a bare boolean — R3 would have nothing to show).
- Grant/membership change for one user → `invalidate_user(user_id)`.
- Grant/membership change touching a team → `invalidate_all()` (blunt, but team-level
  changes are assumed rare; avoids the fan-out problem of tracking which users are
  under which team transitively).
- Cost of this choice: a burst of team-level mutations under load will thrash the whole
  cache and every subsequent check pays a full DB traversal until it's warm again. That's
  the honest cost — say so in README, don't hide it.
- Cold path: recursive query over `team_relationships` with a visited-set (graph has
  cycles per R4's own hint — must not infinite-loop), then resolve grants at every
  subject/resource pair walked, take the highest applicable role.
- R2's 1s bound is satisfied trivially since invalidation is synchronous in-process
  (single backend instance, no pub/sub needed) — call this out explicitly in README,
  it's a "constraint made it easy" moment, not a clever solution.

## Open ambiguities to resolve in README (not block on — decide and document)
- Org grant applying to repos: does an org-level grant get resolved by walking
  `resource.org_id` at check time, or materialized? (Plan: resolve at check time —
  it's one extra join/lookup, not worth precomputing.)
- Does removing a user from a team count as a "grant" for the 1s revocation SLA, or
  only grant-table rows? (Plan: both — anything that changes the derivation is a
  mutation for R2's purposes.)
- Compose resource limits: problem statement says "enforced in the compose file we
  provide" but no compose file was given to us. Plan: we write our own
  `docker-compose.yml` with `deploy.resources.limits` at 2 vCPU / 4GB total across
  services, and say so explicitly in README as our interpretation.
- Cycle handling divergence: oracle without a visited-set will loop forever on cyclic
  team data — either the oracle also needs one (defeats "naive" spirit) or the harness
  must skip/timeout on cyclic subjects and log it as a known divergence source. Decide
  when R4 is built; document the reasoning either way.

## Build order (rough 4h allocation, cut from the bottom if short on time)
- [ ] Schema + migrations (subjects, resources, team_relationships, grants + indexes)
- [ ] Fixture generator (50k users / 4k teams up to 8 levels / 20k repos / ~400k grants)
- [ ] `oracle.py` — naive recursive check, no cache, standalone, readable in one sitting
- [ ] Fast path: `cache.py` (get/set/invalidate_user/invalidate_all) + `checker.py`
      (`check`, `explain`) using the cache
- [ ] API: FastAPI + Pydantic — `/check`, `/explain`, `/orgs`, `/orgs/{id}/repos`,
      `/resource/{id}`, `GET+POST /grant` — OpenAPI schema is the typed contract, have
      frontend consume generated types from it
- [ ] R4 harness: random checks + random mutations interleaved against oracle vs fast
      path, log divergences with which-side-was-wrong reasoning
- [ ] Load generator script (flags: check rate, mutation rate, duration)
- [ ] Frontend: user search + repo/org + action dropdown + check button, explain path
      rendered as breadcrumb, staleness indicator on cache-hit answers
- [ ] docker-compose.yml (postgres + backend + frontend, resource-limited)
- [ ] BENCH.md (p50/p95/p99 from load generator, one named bottleneck)
- [ ] README.md (running instructions, current state, tradeoffs, decisions log)
- [ ] agent-transcripts/ — export as we go, don't do it retroactively at the end

## Status
Nothing built yet — plan only.

## Chosen design (the R1/R2 tradeoff) — resolved
Point picked: **cache only the team-membership path. Grants are always live.**
- Cache key: `subject_id` (a user) → `{team_path: [team_id, team_id, ...], created_at}`
  — the full set of teams (and their ancestors) this user is nested under. No resource,
  no role, no grant data in the cache.
- On check: get user's cached `team_path` (or compute + cache on miss via recursive
  `team_relationships` walk with a visited-set — graph has cycles per R4's hint).
  Then query `grants` live for `{user_id} ∪ team_path` against the target repo *and*
  its `org_id` (climbing one level — no repo-level materialization of org grants, per
  decision below), take the highest role found. This live grant lookup is what makes
  R3's explain trivial and R2's revocation instant: grants are never cached.
- `invalidate_user(user_id)`: called when a user's own team membership changes (added
  to / removed from a team) — deletes just that user's cache entry.
- `invalidate_all()`: called when a team-to-team relationship changes (a team is
  re-parented) — because that can shift the ancestor path for every user nested under
  it, and we don't track that reverse mapping. Blunt, but team-to-team edits are rare.
- **Grant table changes never touch the cache at all** — they're read live every check,
  so a revoked grant is reflected on the very next check, not bounded by any
  invalidation logic. This is the cleanest part of the design: R2's 1s bound is met by
  construction for grants, and only membership changes need explicit invalidation.

25% tradeoff quality · 25% ambiguities surfaced · 25% code quality/typed contract ·

- Commit as you go (real messages) — they read history to verify change-request timing.
- `agent-transcripts/` raw logs — don't clean these up, don't skip messy ones.

## Chosen design (the R1/R2 tradeoff)
Point picked: **cache the resolved path, invalidate coarsely.**
- Cache key: `subject_id` → `{path: [user, team, team, ..., resource], role, created_at}`.
- Cache hit → check is O(1) dict lookup, and the stored path *is* the R3 explanation
  (this is why we don't cache a bare boolean — R3 would have nothing to show).
- Grant/membership change for one user → `invalidate_user(user_id)`.
- Grant/membership change touching a team → `invalidate_all()` (blunt, but team-level
  changes are assumed rare; avoids the fan-out problem of tracking which users are
  under which team transitively).
- Cost of this choice: a burst of team-level mutations under load will thrash the whole
  cache and every subsequent check pays a full DB traversal until it's warm again. That's
  the honest cost — say so in README, don't hide it.
- Cold path: recursive query over `team_relationships` with a visited-set (graph has
  cycles per R4's own hint — must not infinite-loop), then resolve grants at every
  subject/resource pair walked, take the highest applicable role.
- R2's 1s bound is satisfied trivially since invalidation is synchronous in-process
  (single backend instance, no pub/sub needed) — call this out explicitly in README,
  it's a "constraint made it easy" moment, not a clever solution.

  `resource.org_id` at check time, or materialized? (Plan: resolve at check time —
  it's one extra join/lookup, not worth precomputing.)

  only grant-table rows? (Plan: both — anything that changes the derivation is a
  mutation for R2's purposes.)

  services, and say so explicitly in README as our interpretation.

  team data — either the oracle also needs one (defeats "naive" spirit) or the harness

  when R4 is built; document the reasoning either way.

Went through both PDFs again line by line against the plan. Found several real gaps — some are outright bugs in the current design, not just nitpicks.

**Bugs in the current design**

1. **"team_path" as a list is wrong if the graph isn't a strict tree.** The schema (`team_relationships`: subject_id → belongs_to_team_id) allows a subject to have *multiple* parent rows, and nothing in the PDF says a user/team has exactly one parent — "teams nest inside other teams" doesn't rule out a user or team having two independent parents. If that's allowed, "the path" isn't a single chain, it's a *reachable set* of ancestor teams. Cache should hold a **set**, not a path.
2. **That breaks R3 for cache hits.** If the cache only stores a flat set of team IDs, there's no parent-link info to reconstruct "alice → platform-eng → infrastructure → ...". `explain()` can't reuse the cached set — it needs its own fresh walk that tracks parent pointers to produce one concrete chain. Right now the plan says explain does "cache-backed team-path resolution," which only works if we keep the old design. Fix: cache stores the set (for fast boolean checks), `explain()` always does a live walk with parent-tracking, never reads the cache. Slower, but explain isn't in the 5k/sec hot path — only `/check` is.
3. **R3 also requires explaining denies**, not just allows ("for both allows and denies"). "No path found" or "highest role found was read, admin was requested" needs an actual designed response shape — this isn't in the plan yet.

**Likely misread requirement**

4. Re-reading R2's own framing: *"removing one user from one high-level team can invalidate enormous amounts of derived state"* — that's describing a **team-membership** mutation, not a grants-table row. But the spec's load generator is described as applying **"grant mutations at a configurable rate."** If we only mutate the `grants` table in the load/bench script, we never exercise the expensive `invalidate_all()` path at all — meaning our BENCH.md numbers would look artificially great and dodge the exact tension (R1 vs R2) the assignment is built around. I'd include team re-parenting / membership churn in the mutation script, and say explicitly in README that "grant mutation" was interpreted broadly.

**Missed from the fixture generator**

5. R4 says *"the provided graph contains cycles"* — but there's no provided graph, **we write the generator**. So our own generator needs to *deliberately* inject a handful of cyclic team edges (and maybe a couple of other edge cases: a team with no members, a grant at the exact boundary role, etc.), or the "divergences we found" section of the deliverable will have nothing real to report. Easy to forget since a naive generator that only appends children never produces cycles on its own.

**Performance risk not yet decided**

6. Computing the ancestor set on a cache miss via N Python-side round-trips to Postgres will blow the 10ms p95 budget by itself (network latency × depth). Should do it as a single **recursive CTE** (`WITH RECURSIVE`) with a visited-array column to stop at cycles — Postgres doesn't cycle-detect for you. This is worth deciding now since it affects the schema/query design, not just an implementation detail.
7. If FastAPI ends up using a sync DB driver, sync endpoints run in a worker thread pool — meaning the "single dict" cache is now touched by multiple threads and needs a lock around mutation. If we go fully async (asyncpg), this disappears. Worth picking one now rather than debugging a race later.

**Frontend requirement gap**

8. Frontend needs to "browse the org: teams, nesting, repositories, **grants**" — current API list (`/orgs`, `/orgs/{id}/repos`, `/resource/{id}`, `/grant`) has no endpoint to list a team's children/parent or the grants on a resource. Minor since feature completeness isn't scored, but should be a named cut in README rather than silently missing.

I'll update plan.md with these fixes now — mainly items 1–2 (set not path, explain always live), 4 (mutation script scope), 5 (intentional cycles in generator), and 6 (recursive CTE decision).

## Chosen design (the R1/R2 tradeoff) — resolved
Point picked: **cache only the team-membership path. Grants are always live.**
- Cache key: `subject_id` (a user) → `{team_path: [team_id, team_id, ...], created_at}`
  — the full set of teams (and their ancestors) this user is nested under. No resource,
  no role, no grant data in the cache.
- On check: get user's cached `team_path` (or compute + cache on miss via recursive
  `team_relationships` walk with a visited-set — graph has cycles per R4's hint).
  Then query `grants` live for `{user_id} ∪ team_path` against the target repo *and*
  its `org_id` (climbing one level — no repo-level materialization of org grants, per
  decision below), take the highest role found. This live grant lookup is what makes
  R3's explain trivial and R2's revocation instant: grants are never cached.
- `invalidate_user(user_id)`: called when a user's own team membership changes (added
  to / removed from a team) — deletes just that user's cache entry.
- `invalidate_all()`: called when a team-to-team relationship changes (a team is
  re-parented) — because that can shift the ancestor path for every user nested under
  it, and we don't track that reverse mapping. Blunt, but team-to-team edits are rare.
- **Grant table changes never touch the cache at all** — they're read live every check,
  so a revoked grant is reflected on the very next check, not bounded by any
  invalidation logic. This is the cleanest part of the design: R2's 1s bound is met by
  construction for grants, and only membership changes need explicit invalidation.
- Honest cost to state in README: a burst of team-*reparenting* mutations thrashes the
  whole cache; a burst of user-membership mutations only costs cache misses for those
  specific users. Grant mutations cost nothing to cache correctness since they were
  never cached — but they mean every check always pays a live grants query, which is
  the thing the latency budget (p95 <10ms) has to absorb.

# Repository Access Service — Plan

Working doc. Update checkboxes as things get built. Keep entries short.

## Scoring reality check (from instructions)
25% tradeoff quality · 25% ambiguities surfaced · 25% code quality/typed contract ·
15% change-request absorption · 10% BENCH.md. **Feature completeness is not scored.**
So: a sharp README > a fuller feature set. Don't burn the 4h chasing frontend polish
if R1–R4 + README aren't solid.

Hard requirements regardless of scoring weight:
- `docker compose up` from clean clone, no manual steps, must work.
- R4 oracle is required, not optional, and must not share code with the fast path.
- Commit as you go (real messages) — they read history to verify change-request timing.
- `agent-transcripts/` raw logs — don't clean these up, don't skip messy ones.

## Chosen design (the R1/R2 tradeoff) — resolved
Point picked: **cache only the team-membership path. Grants are always live.**
- Cache key: `subject_id` (a user) → `{team_path: [team_id, team_id, ...], created_at}`
  — the full set of teams (and their ancestors) this user is nested under. No resource,
  no role, no grant data in the cache.
- On check: get user's cached `team_path` (or compute + cache on miss via recursive
  `team_relationships` walk with a visited-set — graph has cycles per R4's hint).
  Then query `grants` live for `{user_id} ∪ team_path` against the target repo *and*
  its `org_id` (climbing one level — no repo-level materialization of org grants, per
  decision below), take the highest role found. This live grant lookup is what makes
  R3's explain trivial and R2's revocation instant: grants are never cached.
- `invalidate_user(user_id)`: called when a user's own team membership changes (added
  to / removed from a team) — deletes just that user's cache entry.
- `invalidate_all()`: called when a team-to-team relationship changes (a team is
  re-parented) — because that can shift the ancestor path for every user nested under
  it, and we don't track that reverse mapping. Blunt, but team-to-team edits are rare.
- **Grant table changes never touch the cache at all** — they're read live every check,
  so a revoked grant is reflected on the very next check, not bounded by any
  invalidation logic. This is the cleanest part of the design: R2's 1s bound is met by
  construction for grants, and only membership changes need explicit invalidation.
- Honest cost to state in README: a burst of team-*reparenting* mutations thrashes the
  whole cache; a burst of user-membership mutations only costs cache misses for those
  specific users. Grant mutations cost nothing to cache correctness since they were
  never cached — but they mean every check always pays a live grants query, which is
  the thing the latency budget (p95 <10ms) has to absorb.

## Ambiguities — resolved
1. **Org grant vs repo grant**: no repo-level materialization. Check climbs from
   repo → its `org_id` live, compares grants at both levels, takes the highest role.
2. **What invalidates cache**: only user↔team membership changes invalidate that
   user's cache entry (`invalidate_user`). Grant table rows never touch the cache —
   they're not cached, so nothing to invalidate. Team↔team reparenting → `invalidate_all`
   (see above).
3. **No provided compose file with limits**: write our own `docker-compose.yml` plus
   a `Dockerfile` per service (backend, frontend), with `deploy.resources.limits` set
   to 2 vCPU / 4GB total across services.
4. **Oracle cycle handling**: oracle keeps a visited-set too (a naive traversal that
   infinite-loops on the provided cyclic data isn't "correct," just broken — a
   visited-set doesn't add cleverness, it's required for the oracle to terminate).
   Build order: get R1/R2/R3 solid first: oracle + R4 harness comes after.

## Process
Build step by step, one reviewable chunk at a time — no one-shot generation of the
whole backend. Each step below is a checkpoint: implement, show diff, get a go-ahead,
move on.

## Build order (cut from the bottom if short on time)
- [ ] Schema + migrations (subjects, resources, team_relationships, grants + indexes)
- [ ] Fixture generator (50k users / 4k teams up to 8 levels / 20k repos / ~400k grants)
- [ ] `cache.py` — get/set/invalidate_user/invalidate_all, dict-backed
- [ ] `checker.py` — `check(user, action, repo)` and `explain(user, action, repo)`,
      cache-backed team-path resolution + live grants query (this is R1 + R3 together)
- [ ] Grant mutation endpoint wired to `invalidate_user` — this is R2
- [ ] API: FastAPI + Pydantic — `/check`, `/explain`, `/orgs`, `/orgs/{id}/repos`,
      `/resource/{id}`, `GET+POST /grant` — OpenAPI schema is the typed contract, have
      frontend consume generated types from it
- [ ] `oracle.py` — naive recursive check with visited-set, standalone, no shared code
      with checker.py, readable in one sitting
- [ ] R4 harness: random checks + random mutations interleaved against oracle vs fast
      path, log divergences with which-side-was-wrong reasoning
- [ ] Load generator script (flags: check rate, mutation rate, duration)
- [ ] Frontend: user search + repo/org + action dropdown + check button, explain path
      rendered as breadcrumb, staleness indicator on cache-hit answers
- [ ] docker-compose.yml + Dockerfiles (postgres + backend + frontend, resource-limited)
- [ ] BENCH.md (p50/p95/p99 from load generator, one named bottleneck)
- [ ] README.md (running instructions, current state, tradeoffs, decisions log)
- [ ] agent-transcripts/ — export as we go, don't do it retroactively at the end

## Status
Nothing built yet — plan only. Next up: schema + migrations.

## Technical decisions (to avoid finding out the hard way mid-build)
- **Ancestor-set computation on cache miss uses a single `WITH RECURSIVE` CTE**, not an
  app-level loop doing one round-trip per depth level — at unbounded depth, N network
  round trips alone can blow the 10ms p95 budget before any real work happens.
  Postgres does **not** cycle-detect recursive CTEs on its own — carry a visited-array
  column and stop expanding a branch once a team_id reappears in it (PG14+ has a native
  `CYCLE` clause; use it if available, otherwise the array check).
- **Pick sync or async DB access up front and stick to it.** If FastAPI endpoints stay

# Repository Access Service — Plan

Working doc. Update checkboxes as things get built. Keep entries short.

## Scoring reality check (from instructions)
25% tradeoff quality · 25% ambiguities surfaced · 25% code quality/typed contract ·
15% change-request absorption · 10% BENCH.md. **Feature completeness is not scored.**
So: a sharp README > a fuller feature set. Don't burn the 4h chasing frontend polish
if R1–R4 + README aren't solid.

Hard requirements regardless of scoring weight:
- `docker compose up` from clean clone, no manual steps, must work.
- R4 oracle is required, not optional, and must not share code with the fast path.
- Commit as you go (real messages) — they read history to verify change-request timing.
- `agent-transcripts/` raw logs — don't clean these up, don't skip messy ones.

## Chosen design (the R1/R2 tradeoff) — resolved
Point picked: **cache only the reachable team set. Grants are always live.**
- Cache key: `subject_id` (a user) → `{team_ids: set(...), created_at}` — the full set
  of teams this user is transitively a member of. **A set, not a "path"**: the schema
  (`team_relationships` is a row per edge) doesn't guarantee a subject has exactly one
  parent, so a user can land in more than one branch. No resource, role, or grant data
  in the cache.
- On check: get user's cached `team_ids` (or compute + cache on miss — see recursive
  CTE decision below, must use a visited-set / cycle guard). Query `grants` live for
  `{user_id} ∪ team_ids` against the target repo *and* its `org_id` (climbing one
  level — no repo-level materialization of org grants), take the highest role found.
  Grants are never cached, so a revoked grant is reflected on the very next check —
  R2's 1s bound is met by construction for grants.
- `invalidate_user(user_id)`: user's own membership changes → delete just that user's
  entry.
- `invalidate_all()`: a team-to-team edge changes (re-parenting) → can shift the
  ancestor set for every user nested under it, and we don't track that reverse
  mapping, so wipe everything. Blunt, but team-to-team edits are assumed rare.
- **`explain()` never reads the cache.** A flat set has no parent-links, so it can't
  produce "alice → platform-eng → infrastructure → ..." — explain always does a fresh
  walk that tracks parent-of-each-team-visited, to reconstruct one concrete chain.
  This is fine: explain isn't in the 5k/sec hot path, only `/check` is.
- `explain()` must also cover **denies**, not just allows: "no path reaches this
  resource" and "reached it but highest role found (read) is below what was asked
  (admin)" are two different deny shapes — both need a real response, not a bare
  `false`.
- Honest cost for README: a burst of team-reparenting mutations thrashes the whole
  cache; user-membership churn only costs misses for those specific users; grant
  mutations cost nothing to cache correctness (never cached) but mean every check pays
  a live grants query — that's what the 10ms p95 budget actually has to absorb.

## Ambiguities — resolved
1. **Org grant vs repo grant**: no repo-level materialization. Check climbs from
   repo → its `org_id` live, compares grants at both levels, takes the highest role.
2. **What invalidates cache**: only user↔team membership changes invalidate that
   user's cache entry (`invalidate_user`). Grant table rows never touch the cache —
   they're not cached, so nothing to invalidate. Team↔team reparenting → `invalidate_all`
   (see above).
3. **No provided compose file with limits**: write our own `docker-compose.yml` plus
   a `Dockerfile` per service (backend, frontend), with `deploy.resources.limits` set
   to 2 vCPU / 4GB total across services.
4. **Oracle cycle handling**: oracle keeps a visited-set too (a naive traversal that
   infinite-loops on the provided cyclic data isn't "correct," just broken — a
   visited-set doesn't add cleverness, it's required for the oracle to terminate).
   Build order: get R1/R2/R3 solid first: oracle + R4 harness comes after.

## Process
Build step by step, one reviewable chunk at a time — no one-shot generation of the
whole backend. Each step below is a checkpoint: implement, show diff, get a go-ahead,
move on.

## Build order (cut from the bottom if short on time)
- [ ] Schema + migrations (subjects, resources, team_relationships, grants + indexes)
- [ ] Fixture generator (50k users / 4k teams up to 8 levels / 20k repos / ~400k grants)
- [ ] `cache.py` — get/set/invalidate_user/invalidate_all, dict-backed
- [ ] `checker.py` — `check(user, action, repo)` and `explain(user, action, repo)`,
      cache-backed team-path resolution + live grants query (this is R1 + R3 together)
- [ ] Grant mutation endpoint wired to `invalidate_user` — this is R2
- [ ] API: FastAPI + Pydantic — `/check`, `/explain`, `/orgs`, `/orgs/{id}/repos`,
      `/resource/{id}`, `GET+POST /grant` — OpenAPI schema is the typed contract, have
      frontend consume generated types from it
- [ ] `oracle.py` — naive recursive check with visited-set, standalone, no shared code
      with checker.py, readable in one sitting
- [ ] R4 harness: random checks + random mutations interleaved against oracle vs fast
      path, log divergences with which-side-was-wrong reasoning
- [ ] Load generator script (flags: check rate, mutation rate, duration)
- [ ] Frontend: user search + repo/org + action dropdown + check button, explain path
      rendered as breadcrumb, staleness indicator on cache-hit answers
- [ ] docker-compose.yml + Dockerfiles (postgres + backend + frontend, resource-limited)
- [ ] BENCH.md (p50/p95/p99 from load generator, one named bottleneck)
- [ ] README.md (running instructions, current state, tradeoffs, decisions log)
- [ ] agent-transcripts/ — export as we go, don't do it retroactively at the end

## Status
Nothing built yet — plan only. Next up: schema + migrations.

  R2's 1s bound is met by construction for grants.
- `invalidate_user(user_id)`: user's own membership changes → delete just that user's
  entry.
- `invalidate_all()`: a team-to-team edge changes (re-parenting) → can shift the
  ancestor set for every user nested under it, and we don't track that reverse
  mapping, so wipe everything. Blunt, but team-to-team edits are assumed rare.
- **`explain()` never reads the cache.** A flat set has no parent-links, so it can't
  produce "alice → platform-eng → infrastructure → ..." — explain always does a fresh
  walk that tracks parent-of-each-team-visited, to reconstruct one concrete chain.
  This is fine: explain isn't in the 5k/sec hot path, only `/check` is.

  resource" and "reached it but highest role found (read) is below what was asked
  (admin)" are two different deny shapes — both need a real response, not a bare
  `false`.

  cache; user-membership churn only costs misses for those specific users; grant
  mutations cost nothing to cache correctness (never cached) but mean every check pays
  a live grants query — that's what the 10ms p95 budget actually has to absorb.

1. **Org grant vs repo grant**: no repo-level materialization. Check climbs from
   repo → its `org_id` live, compares grants at both levels, takes the highest role.
2. **What invalidates cache**: only user↔team membership changes invalidate that
   user's cache entry (`invalidate_user`). Grant table rows never touch the cache —
   they're not cached, so nothing to invalidate. Team↔team reparenting → `invalidate_all`
   (see above).

   a `Dockerfile` per service (backend, frontend), with `deploy.resources.limits` set
   to 2 vCPU / 4GB total across services.
4. **Oracle cycle handling**: oracle keeps a visited-set too (a naive traversal that
   infinite-loops on the provided cyclic data isn't "correct," just broken — a
   visited-set doesn't add cleverness, it's required for the oracle to terminate).
   Build order: get R1/R2/R3 solid first: oracle + R4 harness comes after.

## Technical decisions (to avoid finding out the hard way mid-build)
- **Ancestor-set computation on cache miss uses a single `WITH RECURSIVE` CTE**, not an
  app-level loop doing one round-trip per depth level — at unbounded depth, N network
  round trips alone can blow the 10ms p95 budget before any real work happens.
  Postgres does **not** cycle-detect recursive CTEs on its own — carry a visited-array
  column and stop expanding a branch once a team_id reappears in it (PG14+ has a native
  `CYCLE` clause; use it if available, otherwise the array check).
- **Pick sync or async DB access up front and stick to it.** If FastAPI endpoints stay
  sync (e.g. psycopg2 + SQLAlchemy), they run in a worker thread pool — meaning the
  cache dict is touched by multiple threads and needs a lock around mutation. Going
  async (asyncpg) avoids this entirely since there's one event loop. Decide before
  writing `cache.py`, not after a race shows up.
- **Fixture generator must deliberately inject cycles.** R4 talks about "the provided
  graph contains cycles" — there is no provided graph, we write the generator, so if it
  only ever appends children it will never produce one on its own. Inject a small,
  known number of cyclic team edges (and note them) so the R4 harness has something
  real to find, rather than discovering post-hoc that there's nothing to report.
- **Load generator's "grant mutations" should include team membership changes, not
  just grants-table rows.** R2's own example of the hard case is "removing one user
  from one high-level team" — a membership edit, not a grants CRUD op. If the mutation
  script only touches `grants`, it never exercises `invalidate_all()`, and BENCH.md
  numbers would look better than the design actually costs under the scenario the
  assignment is built around. State this interpretation explicitly in README.

## Risks / what could still go wrong
- Deep + wide ancestor sets (a user in many overlapping branches) could make the live
  grants query (`subject_id IN (...)`) large enough to matter at p95 — worth checking
  actual set sizes the fixture produces, not just assuming 8 levels means 8 rows.
- `invalidate_all()` under concurrent load: if the harness or load generator fires
  team-reparenting mutations frequently, the cache may spend most of its time cold,
  and p95 will reflect worst-case (cold) latency more than steady-state. If that
  happens, it's the honest cost of the chosen tradeoff — report it in BENCH.md, don't
  quietly tune the mutation rate down to hide it.
- Cyclic fixture data reaching the fast path: the recursive CTE's cycle guard and the
  oracle's visited-set need to agree on *what counts as visited* (team_id only, or
  team_id + which parent edge), or they can diverge on cyclic subjects for reasons
  that are really a modeling disagreement, not a bug — decide and document when R4 is
  built.
- Single-instance-only assumption (no Redis, in-process dict cache) means this design
  does not survive a second backend replica — fine per the constraints, but worth one
  line in README's tradeoffs so it's clear this was a choice, not an oversight.

## Process
Build step by step, one reviewable chunk at a time — no one-shot generation of the
whole backend. Each step below is a checkpoint: implement, show diff, get a go-ahead,
move on.

- [ ] Fixture generator (50k users / 4k teams up to 8 levels / 20k repos / ~400k grants)
- [ ] `cache.py` — get/set/invalidate_user/invalidate_all, dict-backed
- [ ] `checker.py` — `check(user, action, repo)` and `explain(user, action, repo)`,

- [ ] Grant mutation endpoint wired to `invalidate_user` — this is R2
- [ ] API: FastAPI + Pydantic — `/check`, `/explain`, `/orgs`, `/orgs/{id}/repos`,

      frontend consume generated types from it

      with checker.py, readable in one sitting
- [ ] R4 harness: random checks + random mutations interleaved against oracle vs fast
      path, log divergences with which-side-was-wrong reasoning
- [ ] Load generator script (flags: check rate, mutation rate, duration)
- [ ] Frontend: user search + repo/org + action dropdown + check button, explain path

- [ ] BENCH.md (p50/p95/p99 from load generator, one named bottleneck)
- [ ] README.md (running instructions, current state, tradeoffs, decisions log)

# Repository Access Service — Plan

Working doc. Update checkboxes as things get built. Keep entries short.

## Scoring reality check (from instructions)
25% tradeoff quality · 25% ambiguities surfaced · 25% code quality/typed contract ·
15% change-request absorption · 10% BENCH.md. **Feature completeness is not scored.**
So: a sharp README > a fuller feature set. Don't burn the 4h chasing frontend polish
if R1–R4 + README aren't solid.

Hard requirements regardless of scoring weight:
- `docker compose up` from clean clone, no manual steps, must work.
- R4 oracle is required, not optional, and must not share code with the fast path.
- Commit as you go (real messages) — they read history to verify change-request timing.
- `agent-transcripts/` raw logs — don't clean these up, don't skip messy ones.

## Chosen design (the R1/R2 tradeoff) — resolved
Point picked: **cache only the reachable team set. Grants are always live.**
- Cache key: `subject_id` (a user) → `{team_ids: set(...), created_at}` — the full set
  of teams this user is transitively a member of. **A set, not a "path"**: the schema
  (`team_relationships` is a row per edge) doesn't guarantee a subject has exactly one
  parent, so a user can land in more than one branch. No resource, role, or grant data
  in the cache.
- On check: get user's cached `team_ids` (or compute + cache on miss — see recursive
  CTE decision below, must use a visited-set / cycle guard). Query `grants` live for
  `{user_id} ∪ team_ids` against the target repo *and* its `org_id` (climbing one
  level — no repo-level materialization of org grants), take the highest role found.
  Grants are never cached, so a revoked grant is reflected on the very next check —
  R2's 1s bound is met by construction for grants.
- `invalidate_user(user_id)`: user's own membership changes → delete just that user's
  entry.
- `invalidate_all()`: a team-to-team edge changes (re-parenting) → can shift the
  ancestor set for every user nested under it, and we don't track that reverse
  mapping, so wipe everything. Blunt, but team-to-team edits are assumed rare.
- **`explain()` never reads the cache.** A flat set has no parent-links, so it can't
  produce "alice → platform-eng → infrastructure → ..." — explain always does a fresh
  walk that tracks parent-of-each-team-visited, to reconstruct one concrete chain.
  This is fine: explain isn't in the 5k/sec hot path, only `/check` is.
- `explain()` must also cover **denies**, not just allows: "no path reaches this
  resource" and "reached it but highest role found (read) is below what was asked
  (admin)" are two different deny shapes — both need a real response, not a bare
  `false`.
- Honest cost for README: a burst of team-reparenting mutations thrashes the whole
  cache; user-membership churn only costs misses for those specific users; grant
  mutations cost nothing to cache correctness (never cached) but mean every check pays
  a live grants query — that's what the 10ms p95 budget actually has to absorb.

## Ambiguities — resolved
1. **Org grant vs repo grant**: no repo-level materialization. Check climbs from
   repo → its `org_id` live, compares grants at both levels, takes the highest role.
2. **What invalidates cache**: only user↔team membership changes invalidate that
   user's cache entry (`invalidate_user`). Grant table rows never touch the cache —
   they're not cached, so nothing to invalidate. Team↔team reparenting → `invalidate_all`
   (see above).
3. **No provided compose file with limits**: write our own `docker-compose.yml` plus
   a `Dockerfile` per service (backend, frontend), with `deploy.resources.limits` set
   to 2 vCPU / 4GB total across services.
4. **Oracle cycle handling**: oracle keeps a visited-set too (a naive traversal that
   infinite-loops on the provided cyclic data isn't "correct," just broken — a
   visited-set doesn't add cleverness, it's required for the oracle to terminate).
   Build order: get R1/R2/R3 solid first: oracle + R4 harness comes after.

## Technical decisions (to avoid finding out the hard way mid-build)
- **Ancestor-set computation on cache miss uses a single `WITH RECURSIVE` CTE**, not an
  app-level loop doing one round-trip per depth level — at unbounded depth, N network
  round trips alone can blow the 10ms p95 budget before any real work happens.
  Postgres does **not** cycle-detect recursive CTEs on its own — carry a visited-array
  column and stop expanding a branch once a team_id reappears in it (PG14+ has a native
  `CYCLE` clause; use it if available, otherwise the array check).
- **Pick sync or async DB access up front and stick to it.** If FastAPI endpoints stay
  sync (e.g. psycopg2 + SQLAlchemy), they run in a worker thread pool — meaning the
  cache dict is touched by multiple threads and needs a lock around mutation. Going
  async (asyncpg) avoids this entirely since there's one event loop. Decide before
  writing `cache.py`, not after a race shows up.
- **Fixture generator must deliberately inject cycles.** R4 talks about "the provided
  graph contains cycles" — there is no provided graph, we write the generator, so if it
  only ever appends children it will never produce one on its own. Inject a small,
  known number of cyclic team edges (and note them) so the R4 harness has something
  real to find, rather than discovering post-hoc that there's nothing to report.
- **Load generator's "grant mutations" should include team membership changes, not
  just grants-table rows.** R2's own example of the hard case is "removing one user
  from one high-level team" — a membership edit, not a grants CRUD op. If the mutation
  script only touches `grants`, it never exercises `invalidate_all()`, and BENCH.md
  numbers would look better than the design actually costs under the scenario the
  assignment is built around. State this interpretation explicitly in README.

  actual set sizes the fixture produces, not just assuming 8 levels means 8 rows.

- Cyclic fixture data reaching the fast path: the recursive CTE's cycle guard and the
  oracle's visited-set need to agree on *what counts as visited* (team_id only, or
  team_id + which parent edge), or they can diverge on cyclic subjects for reasons
  that are really a modeling disagreement, not a bug — decide and document when R4 is

- Single-instance-only assumption (no Redis, in-process dict cache) means this design
  does not survive a second backend replica — fine per the constraints, but worth one

# Repository Access Service — Plan

Working doc. Update checkboxes as things get built. Keep entries short.

## Scoring reality check (from instructions)
25% tradeoff quality · 25% ambiguities surfaced · 25% code quality/typed contract ·
15% change-request absorption · 10% BENCH.md. **Feature completeness is not scored.**
So: a sharp README > a fuller feature set. Don't burn the 4h chasing frontend polish
if R1–R4 + README aren't solid.

Hard requirements regardless of scoring weight:
- `docker compose up` from clean clone, no manual steps, must work.
- R4 oracle is required, not optional, and must not share code with the fast path.
- Commit as you go (real messages) — they read history to verify change-request timing.
- `agent-transcripts/` raw logs — don't clean these up, don't skip messy ones.

## Chosen design (the R1/R2 tradeoff) — resolved
Point picked: **cache only the reachable team set. Grants are always live.**
- Cache key: `subject_id` (a user) → `{team_ids: set(...), created_at}` — the full set
  of teams this user is transitively a member of. **A set, not a "path"**: the schema
  (`team_relationships` is a row per edge) doesn't guarantee a subject has exactly one
  parent, so a user can land in more than one branch. No resource, role, or grant data
  in the cache.
- On check: get user's cached `team_ids` (or compute + cache on miss — see recursive
  CTE decision below, must use a visited-set / cycle guard). Query `grants` live for
  `{user_id} ∪ team_ids` against the target repo *and* its `org_id` (climbing one
  level — no repo-level materialization of org grants), take the highest role found.
  Grants are never cached, so a revoked grant is reflected on the very next check —
  R2's 1s bound is met by construction for grants.
- `invalidate_user(user_id)`: user's own membership changes → delete just that user's
  entry.
- `invalidate_all()`: a team-to-team edge changes (re-parenting) → can shift the
  ancestor set for every user nested under it, and we don't track that reverse
  mapping, so wipe everything. Blunt, but team-to-team edits are assumed rare.
- **`explain()` never reads the cache.** A flat set has no parent-links, so it can't
  produce "alice → platform-eng → infrastructure → ..." — explain always does a fresh
  walk that tracks parent-of-each-team-visited, to reconstruct one concrete chain.
  This is fine: explain isn't in the 5k/sec hot path, only `/check` is.
- `explain()` must also cover **denies**, not just allows: "no path reaches this
  resource" and "reached it but highest role found (read) is below what was asked
  (admin)" are two different deny shapes — both need a real response, not a bare
  `false`.
- Honest cost for README: a burst of team-reparenting mutations thrashes the whole
  cache; user-membership churn only costs misses for those specific users; grant
  mutations cost nothing to cache correctness (never cached) but mean every check pays
  a live grants query — that's what the 10ms p95 budget actually has to absorb.

## Ambiguities — resolved
1. **Org grant vs repo grant**: no repo-level materialization. Check climbs from
   repo → its `org_id` live, compares grants at both levels, takes the highest role.
2. **What invalidates cache**: only user↔team membership changes invalidate that
   user's cache entry (`invalidate_user`). Grant table rows never touch the cache —
   they're not cached, so nothing to invalidate. Team↔team reparenting → `invalidate_all`
   (see above).
3. **No provided compose file with limits**: write our own `docker-compose.yml` plus
   a `Dockerfile` per service (backend, frontend), with `deploy.resources.limits` set
   to 2 vCPU / 4GB total across services.
4. **Oracle cycle handling**: oracle keeps a visited-set too (a naive traversal that
   infinite-loops on the provided cyclic data isn't "correct," just broken — a
   visited-set doesn't add cleverness, it's required for the oracle to terminate).
   Build order: get R1/R2/R3 solid first: oracle + R4 harness comes after.

## Technical decisions (to avoid finding out the hard way mid-build)
- **Ancestor-set computation on cache miss uses a single `WITH RECURSIVE` CTE**, not an
  app-level loop doing one round-trip per depth level — at unbounded depth, N network
  round trips alone can blow the 10ms p95 budget before any real work happens.
  Postgres does **not** cycle-detect recursive CTEs on its own — carry a visited-array
  column and stop expanding a branch once a team_id reappears in it (PG14+ has a native
  `CYCLE` clause; use it if available, otherwise the array check).
- **Pick sync or async DB access up front and stick to it.** If FastAPI endpoints stay
  sync (e.g. psycopg2 + SQLAlchemy), they run in a worker thread pool — meaning the
  cache dict is touched by multiple threads and needs a lock around mutation. Going
  async (asyncpg) avoids this entirely since there's one event loop. Decide before
  writing `cache.py`, not after a race shows up.
- **Fixture generator must deliberately inject cycles.** R4 talks about "the provided
  graph contains cycles" — there is no provided graph, we write the generator, so if it
  only ever appends children it will never produce one on its own. Inject a small,
  known number of cyclic team edges (and note them) so the R4 harness has something
  real to find, rather than discovering post-hoc that there's nothing to report.
- **Load generator's "grant mutations" should include team membership changes, not
  just grants-table rows.** R2's own example of the hard case is "removing one user
  from one high-level team" — a membership edit, not a grants CRUD op. Mutation mix:
  membership adds/removes dominate (e.g. ~100 users added to a team per ~5 removed —
  removal is deliberately rarer, matching real orgs), team-to-team reparenting
  (triggers `invalidate_all`) stays rare by design and by mutation-rate weighting —
  don't let the load script fire it often, that's the point of picking this tradeoff.
  State this interpretation explicitly in README.

## Risks — reviewed, decisions locked
- Deep/wide ancestor sets: not worrying about beyond the fixture's 8-level nesting for
  now. Scoped to what we can measure; revisit only if it becomes a real bottleneck.
- `invalidate_all()` staying rare is a design assumption, not just an outcome — the
  load generator's mutation mix is intentionally weighted so team reparenting is
  infrequent (see mutation mix above). This is an accepted limitation of the design:
  it depends on team-level churn actually being rare in practice, and it's called out
  as a real cost in README rather than something the benchmark is tuned to avoid
  showing.
- Cycle detection: `team_id` alone is sufficient for the visited-set/CTE cycle guard,
  both in the fast path and in the oracle. No need for edge-level tracking.
- No Redis / no second cache layer: staying with the single in-process dict on one
  backend instance. Multi-node consistency (keeping two caches in sync) is exactly the
  kind of complexity this assignment's constraints (2 vCPU, no external services) are
  steering away from — adding it would be solving a problem we don't have.

## Process
Build step by step, one reviewable chunk at a time — no one-shot generation of the
whole backend. Each step below is a checkpoint: implement, show diff, get a go-ahead,
move on.

## Build order (cut from the bottom if short on time)
- [ ] Schema + migrations (subjects, resources, team_relationships, grants + indexes)
- [ ] Fixture generator (50k users / 4k teams up to 8 levels / 20k repos / ~400k grants)
      — decide sync/async DB access here too, since the generator hits the same schema.
      Deliberately inject a handful of cyclic team edges + a few edge-case grants
      (boundary roles, org-level-only access, team with no members) so R4 has real
      material.
- [ ] `cache.py` — get/set/invalidate_user/invalidate_all, dict-backed, set-valued
      (lock around mutation only if sync/threaded DB access was chosen above)
- [ ] `checker.py` — `check(user, action, repo)` via recursive-CTE ancestor-set +
      live grants query (R1). `explain(user, action, repo)` does its own live walk
      with parent-tracking, never reads the cache, covers both allow and deny shapes
      (R3)
- [ ] Grant mutation endpoint wired to `invalidate_user` (membership changes) /
      `invalidate_all` (team reparenting) — this is R2
- [ ] API: FastAPI + Pydantic — `/check`, `/explain`, `/orgs`, `/orgs/{id}/repos`,
      `/resource/{id}`, `/resource/{id}/grants`, `/teams/{id}` (parent + children),
      `GET+POST /grant` — OpenAPI schema is the typed contract, have frontend consume
      generated types from it
- [ ] `oracle.py` — naive recursive check with visited-set, standalone, no shared code
      with checker.py, readable in one sitting
- [ ] R4 harness: random checks + random mutations interleaved against oracle vs fast
      path, log divergences with which-side-was-wrong reasoning
- [ ] Load generator script (flags: check rate, mutation rate, duration)
- [ ] Frontend: user search + repo/org + action dropdown + check button, explain path
      rendered as breadcrumb, staleness indicator on cache-hit answers
- [ ] docker-compose.yml + Dockerfiles (postgres + backend + frontend, resource-limited)
- [ ] BENCH.md (p50/p95/p99 from load generator, one named bottleneck)
- [ ] README.md (running instructions, current state, tradeoffs, decisions log)
- [ ] agent-transcripts/ — export as we go, don't do it retroactively at the end

## Status
Nothing built yet — plan only. Next up: schema + migrations.

# Plan

This is our working notes file. We update it as we build. Checkboxes = done or not.

## What actually gets graded

Tradeoffs and ambiguities are worth half the grade combined. Code quality is another
quarter. The change request is 15%. Benchmarks are only 10%. Finishing every feature
isn't graded at all. So we should not rush to build a full frontend if it means the
README is thin. Write things down as we decide them, not at the end.

Things we must not skip no matter what:
- `docker compose up` has to work on a clean machine, no extra steps.
- The oracle (R4) is required. It cannot share code with the fast check path.
- Commit as we go with real messages, so there's a history to read.
- Save the raw agent chat logs into `agent-transcripts/`, don't clean them up.

## The core design: how we're handling checks and revocation

A user can be in multiple teams, and teams can be inside other teams, arbitrarily
deep. So for a given user we compute the full set of teams they're a member of,
directly or through nesting. We cache that set per user.

Grants themselves we never cache. Every check reads the grants table live: we look for
grants belonging to the user or any team in their set, on the target repo or its
parent org, and take the highest role we find. Since grants are always read live, if
someone's access is revoked, the very next check already sees it. No waiting on a
cache to expire.

The cache only needs to be invalidated when someone's team membership changes:
- If a specific user is added to or removed from a team, we just clear that one
  user's cached set.

# Repository Access Service — Plan

Working doc. Update checkboxes as things get built. Keep entries short.

## Scoring reality check (from instructions)
25% tradeoff quality · 25% ambiguities surfaced · 25% code quality/typed contract ·
15% change-request absorption · 10% BENCH.md. **Feature completeness is not scored.**
So: a sharp README > a fuller feature set. Don't burn the 4h chasing frontend polish
if R1–R4 + README aren't solid.

Hard requirements regardless of scoring weight:
- `docker compose up` from clean clone, no manual steps, must work.
- R4 oracle is required, not optional, and must not share code with the fast path.
- Commit as you go (real messages) — they read history to verify change-request timing.
- `agent-transcripts/` raw logs — don't clean these up, don't skip messy ones.

## Chosen design (the R1/R2 tradeoff) — resolved
Point picked: **cache only the reachable team set. Grants are always live.**
- Cache key: `subject_id` (a user) → `{team_ids: set(...), created_at}` — the full set
  of teams this user is transitively a member of. **A set, not a "path"**: the schema
  (`team_relationships` is a row per edge) doesn't guarantee a subject has exactly one
  parent, so a user can land in more than one branch. No resource, role, or grant data
  in the cache.
- On check: get user's cached `team_ids` (or compute + cache on miss — see recursive
  CTE decision below, must use a visited-set / cycle guard). Query `grants` live for
  `{user_id} ∪ team_ids` against the target repo *and* its `org_id` (climbing one
  level — no repo-level materialization of org grants), take the highest role found.
  Grants are never cached, so a revoked grant is reflected on the very next check —
  R2's 1s bound is met by construction for grants.
- `invalidate_user(user_id)`: user's own membership changes → delete just that user's
  entry.
- `invalidate_all()`: a team-to-team edge changes (re-parenting) → can shift the
  ancestor set for every user nested under it, and we don't track that reverse
  mapping, so wipe everything. Blunt, but team-to-team edits are assumed rare.
- **`explain()` never reads the cache.** A flat set has no parent-links, so it can't
  produce "alice → platform-eng → infrastructure → ..." — explain always does a fresh
  walk that tracks parent-of-each-team-visited, to reconstruct one concrete chain.
  This is fine: explain isn't in the 5k/sec hot path, only `/check` is.
- `explain()` must also cover **denies**, not just allows: "no path reaches this
  resource" and "reached it but highest role found (read) is below what was asked
  (admin)" are two different deny shapes — both need a real response, not a bare
  `false`.
- Honest cost for README: a burst of team-reparenting mutations thrashes the whole
  cache; user-membership churn only costs misses for those specific users; grant
  mutations cost nothing to cache correctness (never cached) but mean every check pays
  a live grants query — that's what the 10ms p95 budget actually has to absorb.

## Ambiguities — resolved
1. **Org grant vs repo grant**: no repo-level materialization. Check climbs from
   repo → its `org_id` live, compares grants at both levels, takes the highest role.
2. **What invalidates cache**: only user↔team membership changes invalidate that
   user's cache entry (`invalidate_user`). Grant table rows never touch the cache —
   they're not cached, so nothing to invalidate. Team↔team reparenting → `invalidate_all`
   (see above).
3. **No provided compose file with limits**: write our own `docker-compose.yml` plus
   a `Dockerfile` per service (backend, frontend), with `deploy.resources.limits` set
   to 2 vCPU / 4GB total across services.
4. **Oracle cycle handling**: oracle keeps a visited-set too (a naive traversal that
   infinite-loops on the provided cyclic data isn't "correct," just broken — a
   visited-set doesn't add cleverness, it's required for the oracle to terminate).
   Build order: get R1/R2/R3 solid first: oracle + R4 harness comes after.

## Technical decisions (to avoid finding out the hard way mid-build)
- **Ancestor-set computation on cache miss uses a single `WITH RECURSIVE` CTE**, not an
  app-level loop doing one round-trip per depth level — at unbounded depth, N network
  round trips alone can blow the 10ms p95 budget before any real work happens.
  Postgres does **not** cycle-detect recursive CTEs on its own — carry a visited-array
  column and stop expanding a branch once a team_id reappears in it (PG14+ has a native
  `CYCLE` clause; use it if available, otherwise the array check).
- **Pick sync or async DB access up front and stick to it.** If FastAPI endpoints stay
  sync (e.g. psycopg2 + SQLAlchemy), they run in a worker thread pool — meaning the
  cache dict is touched by multiple threads and needs a lock around mutation. Going
  async (asyncpg) avoids this entirely since there's one event loop. Decide before
  writing `cache.py`, not after a race shows up.
- **Fixture generator must deliberately inject cycles.** R4 talks about "the provided
  graph contains cycles" — there is no provided graph, we write the generator, so if it
  only ever appends children it will never produce one on its own. Inject a small,
  known number of cyclic team edges (and note them) so the R4 harness has something
  real to find, rather than discovering post-hoc that there's nothing to report.
- **Load generator's "grant mutations" should include team membership changes, not
  just grants-table rows.** R2's own example of the hard case is "removing one user
  from one high-level team" — a membership edit, not a grants CRUD op. Mutation mix:
  membership adds/removes dominate (e.g. ~100 users added to a team per ~5 removed —
  removal is deliberately rarer, matching real orgs), team-to-team reparenting
  (triggers `invalidate_all`) stays rare by design and by mutation-rate weighting —
  don't let the load script fire it often, that's the point of picking this tradeoff.
  State this interpretation explicitly in README.

## Risks — reviewed, decisions locked
- Deep/wide ancestor sets: not worrying about beyond the fixture's 8-level nesting for
  now. Scoped to what we can measure; revisit only if it becomes a real bottleneck.
- `invalidate_all()` staying rare is a design assumption, not just an outcome — the
  load generator's mutation mix is intentionally weighted so team reparenting is
  infrequent (see mutation mix above). This is an accepted limitation of the design:
  it depends on team-level churn actually being rare in practice, and it's called out
  as a real cost in README rather than something the benchmark is tuned to avoid
  showing.
- Cycle detection: `team_id` alone is sufficient for the visited-set/CTE cycle guard,
  both in the fast path and in the oracle. No need for edge-level tracking.
- No Redis / no second cache layer: staying with the single in-process dict on one
  backend instance. Multi-node consistency (keeping two caches in sync) is exactly the
  kind of complexity this assignment's constraints (2 vCPU, no external services) are
  steering away from — adding it would be solving a problem we don't have.

## Process
Build step by step, one reviewable chunk at a time — no one-shot generation of the
whole backend. Each step below is a checkpoint: implement, show diff, get a go-ahead,
move on.

## Build order (cut from the bottom if short on time)
- [ ] Schema + migrations (subjects, resources, team_relationships, grants + indexes)
- [ ] Fixture generator (50k users / 4k teams up to 8 levels / 20k repos / ~400k grants)
      — decide sync/async DB access here too, since the generator hits the same schema.
      Deliberately inject a handful of cyclic team edges + a few edge-case grants
      (boundary roles, org-level-only access, team with no members) so R4 has real
      material.
- [ ] `cache.py` — get/set/invalidate_user/invalidate_all, dict-backed, set-valued
      (lock around mutation only if sync/threaded DB access was chosen above)
- [ ] `checker.py` — `check(user, action, repo)` via recursive-CTE ancestor-set +
      live grants query (R1). `explain(user, action, repo)` does its own live walk
      with parent-tracking, never reads the cache, covers both allow and deny shapes
      (R3)
- [ ] Grant mutation endpoint wired to `invalidate_user` (membership changes) /
      `invalidate_all` (team reparenting) — this is R2
- [ ] API: FastAPI + Pydantic — `/check`, `/explain`, `/orgs`, `/orgs/{id}/repos`,
      `/resource/{id}`, `/resource/{id}/grants`, `/teams/{id}` (parent + children),
      `GET+POST /grant` — OpenAPI schema is the typed contract, have frontend consume
      generated types from it
- [ ] `oracle.py` — naive recursive check with visited-set, standalone, no shared code
      with checker.py, readable in one sitting
- [ ] R4 harness: random checks + random mutations interleaved against oracle vs fast
      path, log divergences with which-side-was-wrong reasoning
- [ ] Load generator script (flags: check rate, mutation rate, duration)
- [ ] Frontend: user search + repo/org + action dropdown + check button, explain path
      rendered as breadcrumb, staleness indicator on cache-hit answers
- [ ] docker-compose.yml + Dockerfiles (postgres + backend + frontend, resource-limited)
- [ ] BENCH.md (p50/p95/p99 from load generator, one named bottleneck)
- [ ] README.md (running instructions, current state, tradeoffs, decisions log)
- [ ] agent-transcripts/ — export as we go, don't do it retroactively at the end

## Status
Design decisions locked; `README.md` Tradeoffs section written up from them (keep it
updated as we discuss more, don't let it drift from this file). Nothing built yet.
Next up: schema + migrations.

# Repository Access Service

## Running instructions

Not written yet. Will cover how to run the whole thing and how to run the tests once
there's something to run.

## Current state

Nothing built yet. This section will get updated as pieces land, including anything
that's still broken or missing.

## Requirements and tradeoffs

### How we're balancing fast checks against fast revocation

For every user, we keep track of every team they belong to, including teams nested
inside other teams. That full set gets cached per user.

We never cache grants themselves. Every single check reads the grants table live: we
look for a grant that belongs to the user, or to any team in their cached set, on the
repo being checked or the org that repo belongs to, and we take the best role we find.
Because that lookup is always live, revoking someone's access shows up on their very
next check. There's no delay to reason about there.

The cache only gets cleared in two situations. If one specific user is added to or
removed from a team, we clear just that user's entry. If a team gets moved to sit
under a different parent team, we clear the entire cache, because that single change
can affect everyone nested underneath that team, and we don't keep a reverse map that
would let us figure out exactly who.

That second case is the real cost of this design. We're betting that moving a team
under a new parent is a rare event. If it happened often, the cache would spend a lot
of its time empty, and every check would fall back to the slower live lookup. We think
that's a reasonable bet for how teams actually get restructured in practice, but it is
a bet, and if it's wrong the latency numbers will show it.

We considered caching the actual yes/no answer per user and resource instead. We
decided against it for two reasons: it throws away the information needed to explain
an answer, and a single team change would mean recomputing the answer for every
resource everyone under that team could reach, which is a much bigger blast radius
than what we're doing now.

What would make us reconsider: if we saw evidence that teams get moved around
frequently in practice, we'd want to track which users sit under which team so we
could invalidate just the affected users instead of wiping everything.

### Explaining why an answer is a yes or a no

The explain feature doesn't use the cache. The cache only stores which teams someone
belongs to, not how they got there, so it can't produce a readable trail on its own.
Instead, explain walks the team graph fresh every time, keeps track of the path it
took, and builds a readable chain from that, something like: alice belongs to
platform-eng, which belongs to infrastructure, which has write access to acme-corp,
which covers the api-gateway repo. This is slower than a cache lookup, but that's fine,
because explain isn't part of the 5,000-checks-a-second path. Only the plain check is.

A "no" answer gets the same treatment as a "yes." There are two different reasons
someone could be denied: they have no path to the resource at all, or they do have a
path, but the best role they get from it isn't enough for what they asked to do. Both
of those get shown clearly instead of just returning false.

### Team membership isn't a strict hierarchy

Nothing in the data model guarantees a person or a team has only one parent team. So
we're treating team membership as a graph rather than a strict tree, and we always
keep track of which teams we've already visited while walking it, so we can't get
stuck looping on a cycle.

### Org-level access covers repos underneath it

A grant on an organization applies to every repo in that org. We don't precompute
this. When checking a repo, we also look at grants on its parent org at the same time,
live, and take whichever is higher.

### We're generating the test data ourselves, including the tricky parts

The assignment expects the data to have cycles in team relationships, and it expects
some disagreements between our fast check and a slow, obviously-correct version of it.
Since we're the ones writing the data generator, that only happens if we build it in.
So the generator will include a few teams that loop back on each other, plus some
smaller edge cases like a team with nobody in it, a grant right at a role boundary, and
access that only comes from org-level grants. This gives the comparison step something
real to catch, instead of coming up empty.

### The mutation script moves people between teams, not just grants

The clearest example of a hard revocation case, from the assignment itself, is
removing someone from a large team. That's a membership change, not a row in the
grants table. So our script for generating ongoing changes will add and remove people
from teams, not only add and remove grants. People will be added to teams much more
often than removed (roughly 100 adds for every 5 removes), and moving a team to a new
parent will stay rare on purpose, because that's the case our whole caching approach
is betting stays rare.

### No compose file with resource limits was actually given to us

The assignment refers to a compose file with CPU and memory limits as if we'll be
handed one. We weren't, so we wrote our own, capped at 2 vCPUs and 4GB total.

### No Redis, no second cache

We're running one backend process with one plain in-memory cache. Keeping two caches
in sync across multiple machines is a real problem, but it's not a problem we actually
have here, and adding it anyway would just be extra complexity for no benefit.

### We're only handling the depth our own test data produces

The fixture goes up to 8 levels of team nesting, and that's what we're designing and
testing against. We're not going out of our way to handle something far deeper or
wider than that right now. If it turns out to matter, we'll revisit it.

## Decisions

Not written yet. Will track what we handed to the AI agent versus did ourselves, where
the agent got something wrong, and anything we overrode and why, tied to commits as we
go.

each step. This is fine because explain isn't in the 5k/sec hot path — only `/check`
is under that budget.

Explain also covers **denies**, not just allows — two distinct deny shapes:
- no chain reaches the resource at all, or
- a chain reaches it, but the highest role found is below what was requested.

The schema (`team_relationships`: one row per subject→parent edge) doesn't guarantee a

# Plan

Working notes. Update as we build.

## Grading, in short
- Tradeoffs + ambiguities = half the grade.
- Code quality = another quarter.
- Change request = 15%.
- Benchmarks = only 10%.
- Finishing every feature = not graded at all.
- So: write decisions down as we go, don't rush frontend polish.

## Must not skip
- `docker compose up` works on a clean machine, no manual steps.
- Oracle (R4) is required, and can't share code with the fast path.
- Commit as we go, real messages.
- Save raw agent logs to `agent-transcripts/`.

## The core design
- Cache: per user, the full set of teams they belong to (direct + nested).
- Never cache grants. Always read them live.
- Check = look up grants for `user + their team set`, on the repo or its org, take the highest role.
- Live grants → revocation is instant. No cache to expire.

**Cache invalidation:**
- User added/removed from a team → clear just that user's cache entry.
- Team moved under a new parent → clear the whole cache (can't tell who's affected without a reverse map).

**The bet:** team re-parenting is rare. If it's not, cache goes cold often and latency suffers. We say this plainly in README, not hide it.

**Rejected alternative:** caching the yes/no answer itself. Kills the "why" explain needs, and one team change would mean recomputing every resource every affected user could reach.

## Explain (R3)
- Doesn't use the cache — cache has no "how you got there" info.
- Walks the graph fresh each time, builds the readable chain.
- Fine perf-wise: explain isn't in the 5k/sec path, only check is.
- Denies need explaining too: "no path found" vs "path found, role too low."

## Data decisions
- Team membership is a graph, not a strict tree — nothing stops multiple parents.
- Always track visited teams to avoid infinite loops.
- Org grants apply to repos under them — checked live, not precomputed.
- We write the fixture generator, so cycles in the data are ours to add on purpose (needed for R4 to find anything).
- Also seed a few edge cases: empty team, boundary-role grant, org-only access.
- Mutation script should move people between teams too, not just touch grants — that's the real revocation case R2 is about.
- Adds >> removes >> re-parenting, in that order of frequency (e.g. ~100 adds : 5 removes, re-parenting rare).
- No compose file with limits was given to us — we write our own, capped at 2 vCPU / 4GB.
- No Redis, no second cache. One process, one dict. Syncing two caches is a problem we don't have.
- Only handling nesting up to the fixture's 8 levels for now.
- Cycle check = just track visited team ids, nothing fancier.

## Technical choices (decide early)
- Compute a user's team set in **one recursive SQL query**, not one DB round-trip per level.
- Postgres won't stop a recursive query on a cycle by itself — carry a visited list, cut off repeats.
- Pick sync or async DB access up front. Sync + threadpool means the cache dict needs a lock. Async avoids that.

## Watch out for
- A user in lots of overlapping teams might make the grants lookup bigger than expected — sanity check once fixture exists.
- If the load test ends up moving teams around more than intended, latency will look worse — report it honestly, don't tune it away.

## Build order
Cut from the bottom if short on time.

- [ ] DB schema + indexes
- [ ] Fixture generator (50k users, 4k teams/8 levels, 20k repos, ~400k grants) + planted cycles/edge cases
- [ ] Cache module: get / set / invalidate one user / invalidate all
- [ ] `check()` and `explain()` — this is R1 + R3
- [ ] Grant + membership endpoints wired to invalidation — this is R2
- [ ] Rest of the API (browse orgs/repos/teams/grants), typed contract so FE/BE can't drift
- [ ] Oracle — slow, obviously correct, fully separate code
- [ ] Comparison harness — random checks + mutations, log disagreements
- [ ] Load generator script (check rate, mutation rate flags)
- [ ] Frontend — search user, pick repo + action, see answer + explanation, flag possible staleness
- [ ] docker-compose.yml + Dockerfiles, resource-limited
- [ ] BENCH.md with real numbers
- [ ] Finish README: run instructions, current state, decisions log
- [ ] Keep exporting agent transcripts as we go

## How we're working
Step by step, one reviewable piece at a time. No one-shotting the whole thing.

## Status
Design locked, written into README's tradeoffs section. Nothing built yet.
Next: DB schema.
