# Plan

This is our working notes file. We update it as we build. Checkboxes = done or not.

## What actually gets graded

Tradeoffs and ambiguities are worth half the grade combined. Code quality is another
quarter. The change request is 15%. Benchmarks are only 10%. Finishing every feature
isn't graded at all. So we should not rush to build a full frontend if it means the
README is thin. Write things down as we decide them, not at the end.

Things we must not skip no matter what:
- `docker compose up` has to work on a clean machine, no extra steps.
- The oracle (R4) is required. It cannot share code with the fast check path.
- Commit as we go with real messages, so there's a history to read.
- Save the raw agent chat logs into `agent-transcripts/`, don't clean them up.

## The core design: how we're handling checks and revocation

A user can be in multiple teams, and teams can be inside other teams, arbitrarily
deep. So for a given user we compute the full set of teams they're a member of,
directly or through nesting. We cache that set per user.

Grants themselves we never cache. Every check reads the grants table live: we look for
grants belonging to the user or any team in their set, on the target repo or its
parent org, and take the highest role we find. Since grants are always read live, if
someone's access is revoked, the very next check already sees it. No waiting on a
cache to expire.

The cache only needs to be invalidated when someone's team membership changes:
- If a specific user is added to or removed from a team, we just clear that one
  user's cached set.
- If a team gets moved under a different parent team, we clear the whole cache,
  because that can change the ancestor set for everyone under that team, and we
  don't track that in reverse.

We're betting that team restructuring (a team getting a new parent) is rare. If it
turned out to happen a lot, this cache would spend most of its time cold and we'd feel
it in the latency numbers. That's a real cost, and we'll say so plainly in the README
instead of quietly avoiding it in our own tests.

We considered caching the check result itself (yes/no) instead. We didn't, because a
yes/no answer throws away the "why," and the explain feature needs the why. It also
turns every team change into "recompute for every resource every affected user could
reach," which is worse.

## Explaining a decision (R3)

Explain doesn't use the cache at all. The cache is just a flat set of team ids with no
information about how you got there, so it can't produce a readable chain like
"alice is in platform-eng, which is in infrastructure, which has write on acme-corp,
which covers repo api-gateway." So explain always walks the graph fresh, keeping track
of how it got to each team, and builds the chain from that. This is fine speed-wise
because explain isn't part of the 5,000-checks-per-second path, only the plain check
is.

Explain also needs to answer for a "no" the same way it does for a "yes." A no can
mean two different things: the user has no path to the resource at all, or they have a
path but their highest role there isn't enough for what was asked. Both need to be
shown clearly, not just returned as false.

## Things we decided about the data itself

**Team hierarchy isn't guaranteed to be a clean tree.** The membership table is just a
list of "this subject belongs to this team" rows, and nothing says a person or team
can only have one parent. So we're treating it as a graph, not a tree, and we always
need to track which teams we've already visited while walking it, or we could loop
forever on a cycle.

**Org grants apply to repos underneath them.** We don't precompute that. When checking
a repo, we also look at grants on its parent org, live, every time.

**We're the ones generating the fixture data, not being handed it.** The instructions
mention the data will have cycles in it, but since we're writing the generator
ourselves, that only happens if we make it happen. So the generator will deliberately
plant a handful of cyclic team relationships, plus a few other odd cases (a team with
no members, a grant right at a role boundary, access that only comes from an org and
not a repo), so there's actually something interesting for the oracle-comparison step
to catch.

**The mutation script should move teams around, not just add/remove grants.** The
instructions' own example of a hard revocation case is removing someone from a big
team, which is a membership change, not a row in the grants table. So our load/mutation
script will do membership changes too. Adding people to teams will be common, removing
them from teams will be rarer (something like 100 adds for every 5 removes), and
actually reparenting a team should stay rare, on purpose, to match the bet we made
above.

**Nobody handed us a docker-compose file with resource limits, even though the
instructions imply one exists.** We're writing our own, with the 2 vCPU / 4GB limit
set ourselves.

**We're not adding Redis or a second cache.** One backend process, one plain
in-memory cache. Keeping two caches in sync across machines is a problem we don't
have at this scale, and solving it anyway would just be extra moving parts nobody
asked for.

**We're only worrying about the depth the fixture actually generates (up to 8
levels).** Not going out of our way to handle absurdly deep or wide cases that aren't
in our own data. If it becomes a real problem later, we'll deal with it then.

**Cycle detection just checks team ids we've already seen, nothing fancier.** Both in
the real check path and in the oracle.

## Some technical choices, decided up front so we don't get burned later

- When we need to compute a user's team set from scratch (cache miss), we do it as one
  recursive database query, not by making the app ask the database one level at a
  time. Doing it level by level would rack up a lot of round trips and blow our
  latency budget before we've even done anything else. Postgres doesn't stop itself
  from looping on a cycle in a recursive query, so we carry along a list of visited
  ids and cut off any branch that revisits one.
- We need to decide early whether the backend talks to Postgres synchronously or
  asynchronously, because it affects whether our in-memory cache needs a lock around
  it. If we use a sync driver, FastAPI runs those requests across a pool of threads,
  and multiple threads touching the same cache dictionary needs a lock. Going async
  avoids that problem entirely.

## Still open, to revisit if it becomes real

- If a user ends up in a lot of overlapping teams, the live grants lookup might touch
  more rows than we expect. Worth a quick sanity check once the fixture exists, rather
  than assuming it'll be small.
- If the load test ends up doing more team-reparenting than intended, our numbers will
  look worse, and that's honest — we should report that rather than turning the knob
  down until the numbers look nice.

## Build order

Roughly in this order. If we're running low on time, cut from the bottom.

- [ ] Database schema and indexes
- [ ] Fixture generator (50k users, 4k teams up to 8 levels deep, 20k repos, ~400k
      grants), including the deliberate cycles and edge cases mentioned above
- [ ] Cache module: get / set / invalidate one user / invalidate everything
- [ ] Check function and explain function (this is R1 and R3)
- [ ] Grant and membership endpoints, wired up to call the right invalidation (R2)
- [ ] The rest of the API: browsing orgs, repos, teams, and grants, with a real typed

- [ ] The oracle: a plain, slow, obviously-correct check function, written completely

- [ ] The comparison harness: fires random checks and random mutations at both, logs

- [ ] Load generator script, with flags for check rate and mutation rate
- [ ] Frontend: search a user, pick a repo and an action, see the answer and the
      explanation, and be upfront if the answer could be slightly stale
- [ ] docker-compose.yml and Dockerfiles, resource-limited
- [ ] BENCH.md with real numbers
- [ ] Finish the README: how to run it, what's not done, decisions log
- [ ] Keep exporting agent transcripts as we go

possible to review as we move.

# Repository Access Service

## Running instructions

Not written yet. Will cover how to run the whole thing and how to run the tests once
there's something to run.

## Current state

Nothing built yet. This section will get updated as pieces land, including anything
that's still broken or missing.

## Requirements and tradeoffs

### How we're balancing fast checks against fast revocation

For every user, we keep track of every team they belong to, including teams nested
inside other teams. That full set gets cached per user.

We never cache grants themselves. Every single check reads the grants table live: we
look for a grant that belongs to the user, or to any team in their cached set, on the
repo being checked or the org that repo belongs to, and we take the best role we find.
Because that lookup is always live, revoking someone's access shows up on their very
next check. There's no delay to reason about there.

The cache only gets cleared in two situations. If one specific user is added to or
removed from a team, we clear just that user's entry. If a team gets moved to sit
under a different parent team, we clear the entire cache, because that single change
can affect everyone nested underneath that team, and we don't keep a reverse map that
would let us figure out exactly who.

That second case is the real cost of this design. We're betting that moving a team
under a new parent is a rare event. If it happened often, the cache would spend a lot
of its time empty, and every check would fall back to the slower live lookup. We think
that's a reasonable bet for how teams actually get restructured in practice, but it is
a bet, and if it's wrong the latency numbers will show it.

We considered caching the actual yes/no answer per user and resource instead. We
decided against it for two reasons: it throws away the information needed to explain
an answer, and a single team change would mean recomputing the answer for every
resource everyone under that team could reach, which is a much bigger blast radius
than what we're doing now.

What would make us reconsider: if we saw evidence that teams get moved around
frequently in practice, we'd want to track which users sit under which team so we
could invalidate just the affected users instead of wiping everything.

### Explaining why an answer is a yes or a no

The explain feature doesn't use the cache. The cache only stores which teams someone
belongs to, not how they got there, so it can't produce a readable trail on its own.
Instead, explain walks the team graph fresh every time, keeps track of the path it
took, and builds a readable chain from that, something like: alice belongs to
platform-eng, which belongs to infrastructure, which has write access to acme-corp,
which covers the api-gateway repo. This is slower than a cache lookup, but that's fine,
because explain isn't part of the 5,000-checks-a-second path. Only the plain check is.

A "no" answer gets the same treatment as a "yes." There are two different reasons
someone could be denied: they have no path to the resource at all, or they do have a
path, but the best role they get from it isn't enough for what they asked to do. Both
of those get shown clearly instead of just returning false.

### Team membership isn't a strict hierarchy

Nothing in the data model guarantees a person or a team has only one parent team. So
we're treating team membership as a graph rather than a strict tree, and we always
keep track of which teams we've already visited while walking it, so we can't get
stuck looping on a cycle.

### Org-level access covers repos underneath it

A grant on an organization applies to every repo in that org. We don't precompute
this. When checking a repo, we also look at grants on its parent org at the same time,
live, and take whichever is higher.

### We're generating the test data ourselves, including the tricky parts

The assignment expects the data to have cycles in team relationships, and it expects
some disagreements between our fast check and a slow, obviously-correct version of it.
Since we're the ones writing the data generator, that only happens if we build it in.
So the generator will include a few teams that loop back on each other, plus some
smaller edge cases like a team with nobody in it, a grant right at a role boundary, and
access that only comes from org-level grants. This gives the comparison step something
real to catch, instead of coming up empty.

### The mutation script moves people between teams, not just grants

The clearest example of a hard revocation case, from the assignment itself, is
removing someone from a large team. That's a membership change, not a row in the
grants table. So our script for generating ongoing changes will add and remove people
from teams, not only add and remove grants. People will be added to teams much more
often than removed (roughly 100 adds for every 5 removes), and moving a team to a new
parent will stay rare on purpose, because that's the case our whole caching approach
is betting stays rare.

### No compose file with resource limits was actually given to us

The assignment refers to a compose file with CPU and memory limits as if we'll be
handed one. We weren't, so we wrote our own, capped at 2 vCPUs and 4GB total.

### No Redis, no second cache

We're running one backend process with one plain in-memory cache. Keeping two caches
in sync across multiple machines is a real problem, but it's not a problem we actually
have here, and adding it anyway would just be extra complexity for no benefit.

### We're only handling the depth our own test data produces

The fixture goes up to 8 levels of team nesting, and that's what we're designing and
testing against. We're not going out of our way to handle something far deeper or
wider than that right now. If it turns out to matter, we'll revisit it.

## Decisions

Not written yet. Will track what we handed to the AI agent versus did ourselves, where
the agent got something wrong, and anything we overrode and why, tied to commits as we
go.

# Working preferences for this project

## Writing style (plan.md, README.md, any docs)
- Plain human English. No corporate/AI-sounding text walls.
- Short bullet points over paragraphs. One idea per line.
- Bold/headers for structure, not filler.
- If a section reads like a wall of text, break it up.

## How we build
- Step by step, one reviewable chunk at a time. Never one-shot the whole thing.
- Implement a piece, show it, get a go-ahead, move to the next.
- Keep plan.md updated as we go — what's planned vs what's built.
- Log tradeoffs and decisions into README.md as we make them, not at the end.

## Rules from the assignment brief (still apply)
- No abstraction (interface, factory, plugin system, config layer) used only once —
  ask first if one seems needed.
- Direct implementation over flexible/generic.
- No new dependency unless explicitly asked. Standard library first.
- Every file readable start to end in under 2 minutes.
- Never touch a file not asked about.
- After writing code, briefly explain what each function does and why.
- If a requirement is ambiguous, decide and document it (this is graded), don't
  silently guess — but don't block on things that aren't actually load-bearing either.

## Design decisions locked for this project
See README.md's "Requirements and tradeoffs" section — that's the source of truth,
not this file. Key ones:
- Cache the user's team set, never cache grants — checks read grants live.
- Explain never uses the cache, always walks fresh.
- Team hierarchy treated as a graph, not a tree (cycle-safe everywhere).
- Fixture generator deliberately plants cycles and edge cases.
- No Redis, single in-process cache, one backend instance.

# Plan

Working notes. This file can be as detailed as it needs to be — the "keep it short"
rule in CLAUDE.md only applies to README.md and other docs, not this file. Update
checkboxes and details as we build.

## Grading, in short
- Tradeoffs + ambiguities = half the grade.
- Code quality = another quarter.
- Change request = 15%.
- Benchmarks = only 10%.
- Finishing every feature = not graded at all.
- So: write decisions down as we go, don't rush frontend polish.

## Must not skip
- `docker compose up` works on a clean machine, no manual steps.
- Oracle (R4) is required, and can't share code with the fast path.
- Commit as we go, real messages.
- Save raw agent logs to `agent-transcripts/`.

## The core design
- Cache: per user, the full set of teams they belong to (direct + nested).
- Never cache grants. Always read them live.
- Check = look up grants for `user + their team set`, on the repo or its org, take the highest role.
- Org grants cover their repos, but a repo-level grant can be higher — we always take the max of both, checked live, never precomputed.
- Live grants → revocation is instant. No cache to expire.

**Cache invalidation:**
- User added/removed from a team → clear just that user's cache entry.
- Team moved under a new parent → clear the whole cache (can't tell who's affected without a reverse map).
- Grant added/removed → nothing to invalidate, grants were never cached in the first place.

**The bet:** team re-parenting is rare. If it's not, cache goes cold often and latency suffers. We say this plainly in README, not hide it.

**Rejected alternative:** caching the yes/no answer itself. Kills the "why" explain needs, and one team change would mean recomputing every resource every affected user could reach.

## Explain (R3)
- Doesn't use the cache — cache has no "how you got there" info.
- Walks the graph fresh each time, builds the readable chain.
- Fine perf-wise: explain isn't in the 5k/sec path, only check is.
- Denies need explaining too: "no path found" vs "path found, role too low."

## Data decisions
- Team membership is a graph, not a strict tree — nothing stops multiple parents.
- Always track visited teams to avoid infinite loops.
- We write the fixture generator, so cycles in the data are ours to add on purpose (needed for R4 to find anything).
- Also seed a few edge cases: empty team, boundary-role grant, org-only access, a repo grant that beats its org grant.
- Mutation script should move people between teams too, not just touch grants — that's the real revocation case R2 is about.
- Adds >> removes >> re-parenting, in that order of frequency (e.g. ~100 adds : 5 removes, re-parenting rare).
- No compose file with limits was given to us — we write our own, capped at 2 vCPU / 4GB.
- No Redis, no second cache. One process, one dict. Syncing two caches is a problem we don't have.
- Only handling nesting up to the fixture's 8 levels for now.
- Cycle check = just track visited team ids, nothing fancier.

## Technical choices (decided up front)
- Async DB access throughout (not sync + threadpool) — keeps the in-memory cache single-threaded, no locks needed.
- Raw SQL, no ORM. Small schema, and the recursive CTE for ancestor lookup is easier to reason about as plain SQL than through an ORM abstraction we'd use once.
- Compute a user's team set in **one recursive SQL query**, not one DB round-trip per level.
- Postgres won't stop a recursive query on a cycle by itself — carry a visited list in the query, cut off repeats.

## Watch out for
- A user in lots of overlapping teams might make the grants lookup bigger than expected — sanity check once fixture exists.
- If the load test ends up moving teams around more than intended, latency will look worse — report it honestly, don't tune it away.
- Grant mutations were originally assumed to be the thing needing invalidation — they don't. Only membership mutations do. Make sure the API and mutation scripts reflect that, not the older grant-centric assumption.

---

## File-by-file plan

### Top level
```
repoAccessService/
├── docker-compose.yml
├── backend/
├── frontend/
├── BENCH.md
├── README.md
├── plan.md
├── CLAUDE.md
└── agent-transcripts/
```

### `docker-compose.yml`
- Services: `postgres`, `backend`, `frontend`.
- `postgres`: official image, volume for data, runs `schema.sql` on init.
- `backend`: builds `backend/Dockerfile`, depends on postgres, reads DB connection from env.
- `frontend`: builds `frontend/Dockerfile`, depends on backend.
- `deploy.resources.limits` split across services so the total stays at 2 vCPU / 4GB.

### `backend/Dockerfile`
- Python base image, install `requirements.txt`, copy `app/`, run with uvicorn.

### `backend/requirements.txt`
- fastapi, uvicorn, asyncpg (async Postgres driver — no ORM), pydantic.

### `backend/app/schema.sql`
- Table `subjects`: id, type (user/team), name.
- Table `resources`: id, name, type (org/repo), org_id (nullable, set for repos).
- Table `team_relationships`: id, subject_id, belongs_to_team_id (nullable for a top-level team).
- Table `grants`: id, subject_id, role, resource_id.
- Indexes: `team_relationships(subject_id)`, `team_relationships(belongs_to_team_id)`, `grants(subject_id, resource_id)`, `grants(resource_id)`.

### `backend/app/db.py`
- `get_pool()` — creates/returns the shared asyncpg connection pool, read from env var for the DB URL. One pool for the whole app, created on startup.

### `backend/app/models.py`
- `Role` enum (IntEnum): `READ < WRITE < ADMIN < OWNER`, so comparisons (`role >= action`) just work.
- `CheckResponse` — `{allowed: bool, as_of: datetime}`.
- `ExplainStep` — one hop in the chain (subject name, subject type).
- `ExplainResponse` — `{allowed: bool, chain: list[ExplainStep], granted_role: Role | None, reason: str}`.
- `GrantIn` / `GrantOut` — subject_id, role, resource_id.
- `MembershipIn` — subject_id, belongs_to_team_id.
- `OrgOut`, `RepoOut`, `TeamOut` — basic browse shapes.

### `backend/app/cache.py`
- Module-level dict: `_cache: dict[int, tuple[set[int], datetime]]`.
- `get(user_id) -> set[int] | None` — returns the cached team set, or `None` on a miss.
- `set(user_id, team_ids: set[int])` — stores the set with a timestamp.
- `invalidate_user(user_id)` — deletes that one entry, no-ops if absent.
- `invalidate_all()` — clears the dict.
- No locking needed — async, single event loop, no I/O happens mid-mutation.

### `backend/app/checker.py` — the fast path (R1 + R2 + R3)
- `get_team_set(user_id) -> set[int]` — checks `cache.get`; on a miss, runs the recursive CTE against `team_relationships` (with a visited-array cycle guard), stores the result via `cache.set`, returns it.
- `resolve_role(subject_ids: set[int], repo_id: int) -> Role | None` — one live query against `grants`, matching `subject_id` in `subject_ids` and `resource_id` in `{repo_id, repo's org_id}`. Returns the highest role found, or `None`.
- `check(user_id, action: Role, repo_id: int) -> bool` — `team_set = get_team_set(user_id)`; `role = resolve_role({user_id} | team_set, repo_id)`; return `role is not None and role >= action`.
- `explain(user_id, action: Role, repo_id: int) -> ExplainResponse` — never touches the cache. Walks `team_relationships` from `user_id` outward with its own visited-set, tracking the parent of each team visited. At every subject visited (the user, then each team), checks `grants` against the repo and its org. Picks the highest role found anywhere in the walk and reconstructs the specific chain that produced it (or, on a deny, the closest chain and the role gap, or "no path found" if nothing connects at all).

### `backend/app/oracle.py` — R4, standalone
- Does **not** import anything from `checker.py` or `cache.py`.
- `oracle_check(user_id, action: Role, repo_id: int) -> bool` — plain recursive Python walk over `team_relationships` (one query per level is fine here, it's not perf-critical), visited-set to guard cycles, collects every reachable subject id, queries `grants` directly against the repo and its org, takes the max role, compares to `action`.
- Deliberately simple — short enough to read start to finish and believe it's correct.

### `backend/app/routes.py`
- `GET /check` — `user_id`, `action`, `repo_id` query params → `CheckResponse` via `checker.check`.
- `GET /explain` — same params → `ExplainResponse` via `checker.explain`.
- `GET /orgs` — list resources where type = org.
- `GET /orgs/{id}/repos` — list repos under an org.
- `GET /resource/{id}` — single resource detail.
- `GET /resource/{id}/grants` — grants attached to a resource.
- `GET /teams/{id}` — a team's parent + direct children.
- `GET /grant`, `POST /grant` — list / create grants. **No cache invalidation on this path** — grants are never cached.
- `POST /membership`, `DELETE /membership/{id}` — add/remove a subject from a team. Calls `cache.invalidate_user` if the subject is a user, `cache.invalidate_all` if the subject is a team (re-parenting).

### `backend/scripts/generate_fixture.py`
- `generate_users(n)`, `generate_teams(n, max_depth)`, `generate_repos(n, orgs)`, `generate_grants(n, subjects, resources)`.
- Seeded RNG for reproducibility.
- Deliberately plants: a handful of cyclic team edges, an empty team, a boundary-role grant, an org-only-access repo, a repo grant that overrides its org grant.
- Bulk-inserts into Postgres (batched `INSERT`, not row-by-row) to keep generation fast at this scale.

### `backend/scripts/oracle_harness.py` — R4 harness
- `random_check()` — picks a random `(user_id, action, repo_id)`.
- `random_mutation()` — applies a random grant or membership change, weighted like the load generator's mix.
- `run_harness(num_rounds)` — interleaves checks and mutations, running each check through both `checker.check` and `oracle.oracle_check`, logging any disagreement with enough detail (ids, timing) to investigate afterward.
- Output feeds the "divergences we found" writeup — this script finds them, we explain them by hand.

### `backend/scripts/load_test.py`
- CLI flags: `--check-rate`, `--mutation-rate`, `--duration`, `--url`.
- `run_checks(rate, duration)` — fires `/check` at the target rate, records latency per request.
- `run_mutations(rate, duration)` — fires membership/grant mutations at the target rate, using the same adds-heavy mix as the fixture edge cases.
- Runs both concurrently, reports p50/p95/p99 at the end.

### `backend/tests/`
- `test_cache.py` — get/set/invalidate_user/invalidate_all, plain dict behavior, no mocking.
- `test_checker.py` — real Postgres (test schema), covering: direct grant, team-inherited grant, org-level grant, repo grant overriding org grant, deny (no path), deny (role too low), a cyclic team doesn't hang.
- `test_oracle.py` — same scenarios against `oracle_check`, independently.

### `frontend/Dockerfile`
- Node base image, install deps, build, serve.

### `frontend/src/api.ts`
- Typed fetch wrapper around the backend endpoints. Types kept in sync with the backend's Pydantic models (this is the typed contract requirement) — either hand-written to match or generated from the OpenAPI schema FastAPI already exposes.

### `frontend/src/App.tsx`
- Top-level layout: org/repo browser on one side, check panel on the other.

### `frontend/src/components/CheckPanel.tsx`
- User search input, repo/org dropdown, action dropdown, check button.
- Shows the result plus an "as of" timestamp, and is upfront that a cache-hit answer reflects the cached team set as of that time (grants themselves are always live).

### `frontend/src/components/ExplainView.tsx`
- Renders the chain from `/explain` as a readable breadcrumb, for both allows and denies.

### `frontend/src/components/OrgBrowser.tsx`
- Browse orgs → repos, view a resource's grants, view a team's nesting.

---

## Build order
Cut from the bottom if short on time.

- [ ] `backend/app/schema.sql` + apply to postgres
- [ ] `backend/scripts/generate_fixture.py` (50k users, 4k teams/8 levels, 20k repos, ~400k grants, planted cycles/edge cases)
- [ ] `backend/app/cache.py`
- [ ] `backend/app/checker.py` (`check`, `explain`) — R1 + R3
- [ ] `backend/app/routes.py` — `/check`, `/explain`, `/membership` wired to invalidation — R2
- [ ] rest of `backend/app/routes.py` — browse endpoints, `/grant`
- [ ] `backend/app/oracle.py` — fully separate
- [ ] `backend/scripts/oracle_harness.py` — R4
- [ ] `backend/scripts/load_test.py`
- [ ] `backend/tests/`
- [ ] `frontend/` — CheckPanel, ExplainView, OrgBrowser
- [ ] `docker-compose.yml` + both Dockerfiles, resource-limited
- [ ] `BENCH.md` with real numbers
- [ ] finish `README.md`: run instructions, current state, decisions log
- [ ] keep exporting agent transcripts as we go

## How we're working
Step by step, one reviewable piece at a time. No one-shotting the whole thing.

## Status
Design locked, written into README's tradeoffs section. File-by-file plan written.
Nothing built yet. Next: `backend/app/schema.sql`.

# Plan

Working notes. This file can be as detailed as it needs to be — the "keep it short"
rule in CLAUDE.md only applies to README.md and other docs, not this file. Update
checkboxes and details as we build.

## Grading, in short
- Tradeoffs + ambiguities = half the grade.
- Code quality = another quarter.
- Change request = 15%.
- Benchmarks = only 10%.
- Finishing every feature = not graded at all.
- So: write decisions down as we go, don't rush frontend polish.

## Must not skip
- `docker compose up` works on a clean machine, no manual steps.
- Oracle (R4) is required, and can't share code with the fast path.
- Commit as we go, real messages.
- Save raw agent logs to `agent-transcripts/`.

## The core design
- Cache: per user, the full set of teams they belong to (direct + nested).
- Never cache grants. Always read them live.
- Check = look up grants for `user + their team set`, on the repo or its org, take the highest role.
- Org grants cover their repos, but a repo-level grant can be higher — we always take the max of both, checked live, never precomputed.
- Live grants → revocation is instant. No cache to expire.

**Cache invalidation:**
- User added/removed from a team → clear just that user's cache entry.
- Team moved under a new parent → clear the whole cache (can't tell who's affected without a reverse map).
- Grant added/removed → nothing to invalidate, grants were never cached in the first place.

**The bet:** team re-parenting is rare. If it's not, cache goes cold often and latency suffers. We say this plainly in README, not hide it.

**Rejected alternative:** caching the yes/no answer itself. Kills the "why" explain needs, and one team change would mean recomputing every resource every affected user could reach.

## Explain (R3)
- Doesn't use the cache — cache has no "how you got there" info.
- Walks the graph fresh each time, builds the readable chain.
- Fine perf-wise: explain isn't in the 5k/sec path, only check is.
- Denies need explaining too: "no path found" vs "path found, role too low."

## Data decisions
- Team membership is a graph, not a strict tree — nothing stops multiple parents.
- Always track visited teams to avoid infinite loops.
- We write the fixture generator, so cycles in the data are ours to add on purpose (needed for R4 to find anything).
- Also seed a few edge cases: empty team, boundary-role grant, org-only access, a repo grant that beats its org grant.
- Mutation script should move people between teams too, not just touch grants — that's the real revocation case R2 is about.
- Adds >> removes >> re-parenting, in that order of frequency (e.g. ~100 adds : 5 removes, re-parenting rare).
- No compose file with limits was given to us — we write our own, capped at 2 vCPU / 4GB.
- No Redis, no second cache. One process, one dict. Syncing two caches is a problem we don't have.
- Only handling nesting up to the fixture's 8 levels for now.
- Cycle check = just track visited team ids, nothing fancier.

## Technical choices (decided up front)
- Async DB access throughout (not sync + threadpool) — keeps the in-memory cache single-threaded, no locks needed.
- Raw SQL, no ORM. Small schema, and the recursive CTE for ancestor lookup is easier to reason about as plain SQL than through an ORM abstraction we'd use once.
- Compute a user's team set in **one recursive SQL query**, not one DB round-trip per level.
- Postgres won't stop a recursive query on a cycle by itself — carry a visited list in the query, cut off repeats.

## Watch out for
- A user in lots of overlapping teams might make the grants lookup bigger than expected — sanity check once fixture exists.
- If the load test ends up moving teams around more than intended, latency will look worse — report it honestly, don't tune it away.
- Grant mutations were originally assumed to be the thing needing invalidation — they don't. Only membership mutations do. Make sure the API and mutation scripts reflect that, not the older grant-centric assumption.

+- `invalidate_user(user_id)` — deletes that one entry, no-ops if absent.
+- No locking needed — async, single event loop, no I/O happens mid-mutation.

+- `get_team_set(user_id) -> set[int]` — checks `cache.get`; on a miss, runs the recursive CTE against `team_relationships` (with a visited-array cycle guard), stores the result via `cache.set`, returns it.

+- `resolve_role(subject_ids: set[int], repo_id: int) -> Role | None` — one live query against `grants`, matching `subject_id` in `subject_ids` and `resource_id` in `{repo_id, repo's org_id}`. Returns the highest role found, or `None`.
+- `check(user_id, action: Role, repo_id: int) -> bool` — `team_set = get_team_set(user_id)`; `role = resolve_role({user_id} | team_set, repo_id)`; return `role is not None and role >= action`.

+- `explain(user_id, action: Role, repo_id: int) -> ExplainResponse` — never touches the cache. Walks `team_relationships` from `user_id` outward with its own visited-set, tracking the parent of each team visited. At every subject visited (the user, then each team), checks `grants` against the repo and its org. Picks the highest role found anywhere in the walk and reconstructs the specific chain that produced it (or, on a deny, the closest chain and the role gap, or "no path found" if nothing connects at all).

+- `oracle_check(user_id, action: Role, repo_id: int) -> bool` — plain recursive Python walk over `team_relationships` (one query per level is fine here, it's not perf-critical), visited-set to guard cycles, collects every reachable subject id, queries `grants` directly against the repo and its org, takes the max role, compares to `action`.
+- Deliberately simple — short enough to read start to finish and believe it's correct.
+- `GET /grant`, `POST /grant` — list / create grants. **No cache invalidation on this path** — grants are never cached.

+- `POST /membership`, `DELETE /membership/{id}` — add/remove a subject from a team. Calls `cache.invalidate_user` if the subject is a user, `cache.invalidate_all` if the subject is a team (re-parenting).
+- Deliberately plants: a handful of cyclic team edges, an empty team, a boundary-role grant, an org-only-access repo, a repo grant that overrides its org grant.
+- Bulk-inserts into Postgres (batched `INSERT`, not row-by-row) to keep generation fast at this scale.
+- `random_mutation()` — applies a random grant or membership change, weighted like the load generator's mix.

+- `run_harness(num_rounds)` — interleaves checks and mutations, running each check through both `checker.check` and `oracle.oracle_check`, logging any disagreement with enough detail (ids, timing) to investigate afterward.
+- Output feeds the "divergences we found" writeup — this script finds them, we explain them by hand.
+- `run_checks(rate, duration)` — fires `/check` at the target rate, records latency per request.
+- `run_mutations(rate, duration)` — fires membership/grant mutations at the target rate, using the same adds-heavy mix as the fixture edge cases.
+- Runs both concurrently, reports p50/p95/p99 at the end.
+- `test_cache.py` — get/set/invalidate_user/invalidate_all, plain dict behavior, no mocking.

+- `test_checker.py` — real Postgres (test schema), covering: direct grant, team-inherited grant, org-level grant, repo grant overriding org grant, deny (no path), deny (role too low), a cyclic team doesn't hang.
+- Node base image, install deps, build, serve.

+- Typed fetch wrapper around the backend endpoints. Types kept in sync with the backend's Pydantic models (this is the typed contract requirement) — either hand-written to match or generated from the OpenAPI schema FastAPI already exposes.
+- Top-level layout: org/repo browser on one side, check panel on the other.
+- User search input, repo/org dropdown, action dropdown, check button.
+- Shows the result plus an "as of" timestamp, and is upfront that a cache-hit answer reflects the cached team set as of that time (grants themselves are always live).
+- Renders the chain from `/explain` as a readable breadcrumb, for both allows and denies.
+- Browse orgs → repos, view a resource's grants, view a team's nesting.
+Cut from the bottom if short on time.
+- [ ] `backend/scripts/generate_fixture.py` (50k users, 4k teams/8 levels, 20k repos, ~400k grants, planted cycles/edge cases)
+- [ ] finish `README.md`: run instructions, current state, decisions log
+- [ ] keep exporting agent transcripts as we go
+Step by step, one reviewable piece at a time. No one-shotting the whole thing.
+Design locked, written into README's tradeoffs section. File-by-file plan written.

# Repository Access Service — Plan

Working doc. Update checkboxes as things get built. Keep entries short.

## Scoring reality check (from instructions)
25% tradeoff quality · 25% ambiguities surfaced · 25% code quality/typed contract ·
15% change-request absorption · 10% BENCH.md. **Feature completeness is not scored.**
So: a sharp README > a fuller feature set. Don't burn the 4h chasing frontend polish
if R1–R4 + README aren't solid.

Hard requirements regardless of scoring weight:
- `docker compose up` from clean clone, no manual steps, must work.
- R4 oracle is required, not optional, and must not share code with the fast path.
- Commit as you go (real messages) — they read history to verify change-request timing.
- `agent-transcripts/` raw logs — don't clean these up, don't skip messy ones.

## Chosen design (the R1/R2 tradeoff)
Point picked: **cache the resolved path, invalidate coarsely.**
- Cache key: `subject_id` → `{path: [user, team, team, ..., resource], role, created_at}`.
- Cache hit → check is O(1) dict lookup, and the stored path *is* the R3 explanation
  (this is why we don't cache a bare boolean — R3 would have nothing to show).
- Grant/membership change for one user → `invalidate_user(user_id)`.
- Grant/membership change touching a team → `invalidate_all()` (blunt, but team-level
  changes are assumed rare; avoids the fan-out problem of tracking which users are
  under which team transitively).
- Cost of this choice: a burst of team-level mutations under load will thrash the whole
  cache and every subsequent check pays a full DB traversal until it's warm again. That's
  the honest cost — say so in README, don't hide it.
- Cold path: recursive query over `team_relationships` with a visited-set (graph has
  cycles per R4's own hint — must not infinite-loop), then resolve grants at every
  subject/resource pair walked, take the highest applicable role.
- R2's 1s bound is satisfied trivially since invalidation is synchronous in-process
  (single backend instance, no pub/sub needed) — call this out explicitly in README,
  it's a "constraint made it easy" moment, not a clever solution.

## Open ambiguities to resolve in README (not block on — decide and document)
- Org grant applying to repos: does an org-level grant get resolved by walking
  `resource.org_id` at check time, or materialized? (Plan: resolve at check time —
  it's one extra join/lookup, not worth precomputing.)
- Does removing a user from a team count as a "grant" for the 1s revocation SLA, or
  only grant-table rows? (Plan: both — anything that changes the derivation is a
  mutation for R2's purposes.)
- Compose resource limits: problem statement says "enforced in the compose file we
  provide" but no compose file was given to us. Plan: we write our own
  `docker-compose.yml` with `deploy.resources.limits` at 2 vCPU / 4GB total across
  services, and say so explicitly in README as our interpretation.
- Cycle handling divergence: oracle without a visited-set will loop forever on cyclic
  team data — either the oracle also needs one (defeats "naive" spirit) or the harness
  must skip/timeout on cyclic subjects and log it as a known divergence source. Decide
  when R4 is built; document the reasoning either way.

## Build order (rough 4h allocation, cut from the bottom if short on time)
- [ ] Schema + migrations (subjects, resources, team_relationships, grants + indexes)
- [ ] Fixture generator (50k users / 4k teams up to 8 levels / 20k repos / ~400k grants)
- [ ] `oracle.py` — naive recursive check, no cache, standalone, readable in one sitting
- [ ] Fast path: `cache.py` (get/set/invalidate_user/invalidate_all) + `checker.py`
      (`check`, `explain`) using the cache
- [ ] API: FastAPI + Pydantic — `/check`, `/explain`, `/orgs`, `/orgs/{id}/repos`,
      `/resource/{id}`, `GET+POST /grant` — OpenAPI schema is the typed contract, have
      frontend consume generated types from it
- [ ] R4 harness: random checks + random mutations interleaved against oracle vs fast
      path, log divergences with which-side-was-wrong reasoning
- [ ] Load generator script (flags: check rate, mutation rate, duration)
- [ ] Frontend: user search + repo/org + action dropdown + check button, explain path
      rendered as breadcrumb, staleness indicator on cache-hit answers
- [ ] docker-compose.yml (postgres + backend + frontend, resource-limited)
- [ ] BENCH.md (p50/p95/p99 from load generator, one named bottleneck)
- [ ] README.md (running instructions, current state, tradeoffs, decisions log)
- [ ] agent-transcripts/ — export as we go, don't do it retroactively at the end

## Status
Nothing built yet — plan only.

**Checkbox 1 done: `backend/app/schema.sql`**

What's built:
- 4 tables (`subjects`, `resources`, `team_relationships`, `grants`) matching the plan, with `CHECK` constraints for `type`/`role` instead of separate lookup tables (one less thing, no abstraction for a fixed 2–4 value set).
- 4 indexes matching exactly the queries `checker.py` will run later.

How to test it yourself:
```bash
# one-time
createdb repo_access_test        # or use whatever local Postgres you have

# apply
psql -d repo_access_test -f backend/app/schema.sql

# sanity check
psql -d repo_access_test -c "\d subjects" -c "\d resources" -c "\d team_relationships" -c "\d grants"
```
You should see the 4 tables, the `CHECK` constraints on `type`/`role`, and the 4 named indexes — that's exactly what I verified above against a throwaway local Postgres instance (Docker isn't actually available in this sandbox — `/usr/local/bin/docker` is a broken symlink to a missing `Docker.app`, worth checking that on your end since we'll need it for the final `docker compose up`).

One thing worth a look before you approve: I made `org_id` and `belongs_to_team_id` nullable with no other constraint enforcing "only teams have `belongs_to_team_id` rows" or "only repos have `org_id` set" — that's left to application code (fixture generator + mutation endpoints), not the DB. Fine for a 4-hour scope, but flagging it since it's a place a bug could sneak in later.

Let me know if this looks good — once you approve I'll commit it and move to the fixture generator.

"""Pure graph-building for the team hierarchy fixture. No DB access here on
purpose, so this is easy to read and reason about on its own.
generate_fixture.py calls these and handles the actual database writes.
"""


def build_team_spine(team_ids, depth):
    """First `depth` team ids become a straight chain, root to leaf.

    This guarantees one concrete chain that actually reaches max depth,
    instead of hoping random attachment happens to get there.
    """
    spine = team_ids[:depth]
    edges = [(spine[i], spine[i - 1]) for i in range(1, len(spine))]
    depth_by_team = {team_id: i for i, team_id in enumerate(spine)}
    return edges, depth_by_team


def attach_remaining_teams(rng, team_ids, edges, depth_by_team, max_depth):
    """Every team not already placed gets attached under a random team
    that isn't already at max depth."""
    placed = set(depth_by_team)
    for team_id in team_ids:
        if team_id in placed:
            continue
        eligible = [t for t, d in depth_by_team.items() if d < max_depth - 1]
        parent_id = rng.choice(eligible)
        depth_by_team[team_id] = depth_by_team[parent_id] + 1
        edges.append((team_id, parent_id))
        placed.add(team_id)
    return edges, depth_by_team


def add_second_parents(rng, team_ids, edges, fraction):
    """A handful of teams get a second, independent parent.

    The schema doesn't guarantee one parent per team, so the fixture
    should actually exercise that instead of only ever producing a clean
    tree that hides the case.
    """
    sample_size = int(len(team_ids) * fraction)
    for team_id in rng.sample(team_ids, sample_size):
        other_parent = rng.choice(team_ids)
        if other_parent != team_id:
            edges.append((team_id, other_parent))
    return edges


def plant_cycles(rng, edges, count):
    """Makes a handful of teams cyclic: walks down a few hops from a
    random team and adds an edge back up, so a descendant ends up as its
    own ancestor's parent too.

    R4 expects real cycles to be in the data. Since we write the
    generator ourselves, that only happens if we put them there.
    Returns the new edges plus the (ancestor, descendant) pairs made
    cyclic, so the manifest can record exactly which teams they are.
    """
    children_of = {}
    for child, parent in edges:
        children_of.setdefault(parent, []).append(child)

    planted = []
    candidates = [team for team, kids in children_of.items() if kids]
    for ancestor in rng.sample(candidates, min(count, len(candidates))):
        descendant = ancestor
        for _ in range(rng.randint(2, 5)):
            kids = children_of.get(descendant)
            if not kids:
                break
            descendant = rng.choice(kids)
        if descendant != ancestor:
            edges.append((ancestor, descendant))
            planted.append((ancestor, descendant))
    return edges, planted

"""Generates the fixture data described in plan.md: 50k users, 4k teams
(nested up to 8 levels, with a few deliberate cycles and a multi-parent
case), 1k orgs, 20k repos, and ~400k grants.

Run: python backend/scripts/generate_fixture.py
Needs DATABASE_URL pointing at an empty database with schema.sql already applied.
"""
import asyncio
import json
import os
import random
from pathlib import Path

import asyncpg

from fixture_graph import (
    add_second_parents,
    attach_remaining_teams,
    build_team_spine,
    plant_cycles,
)

DATABASE_URL = os.environ.get(
    "DATABASE_URL", "postgresql://repo_access:repo_access@localhost:5432/repo_access"
)

SEED = 42
NUM_USERS = 50_000
NUM_TEAMS = 4_000
MAX_TEAM_DEPTH = 8
NUM_ORGS = 1_000
NUM_REPOS = 20_000
NUM_GRANTS = 400_000

ROLES = ["read", "write", "admin", "owner"]
ROLE_WEIGHTS = [0.55, 0.25, 0.15, 0.05]  # most access is read, fewest are owner

FIRST_USER_ID = 1
FIRST_TEAM_ID = FIRST_USER_ID + NUM_USERS
FIRST_ORG_ID = 1
FIRST_REPO_ID = FIRST_ORG_ID + NUM_ORGS


def build_teams(rng):
    team_ids = list(range(FIRST_TEAM_ID, FIRST_TEAM_ID + NUM_TEAMS))
    edges, depth_by_team = build_team_spine(team_ids, MAX_TEAM_DEPTH)
    spine_leaf_id = team_ids[MAX_TEAM_DEPTH - 1]
    edges, depth_by_team = attach_remaining_teams(
        rng, team_ids, edges, depth_by_team, MAX_TEAM_DEPTH
    )
    edges = add_second_parents(rng, team_ids, edges, fraction=0.03)
    edges, cyclic_pairs = plant_cycles(rng, edges, count=3)
    empty_team_id = team_ids[-1]  # deliberately gets no direct members
    return team_ids, edges, spine_leaf_id, cyclic_pairs, empty_team_id


def assign_users_to_teams(rng, user_ids, team_ids, spine_leaf_id):
    """Most users get one team, some get two, a few get none. A handful
    are pinned under the deepest team so there's a real deep-nesting case
    to point the load test / benchmark at, not just a hoped-for one."""
    edges = []
    deep_user_ids = rng.sample(user_ids, 20)
    for user_id in deep_user_ids:
        edges.append((user_id, spine_leaf_id))

    for user_id in user_ids:
        roll = rng.random()
        if roll < 0.02:
            continue  # no team at all
        edges.append((user_id, rng.choice(team_ids)))
        if roll > 0.95:
            edges.append((user_id, rng.choice(team_ids)))  # second team
    return edges, deep_user_ids


def build_resources(rng):
    org_ids = list(range(FIRST_ORG_ID, FIRST_ORG_ID + NUM_ORGS))
    repo_ids = list(range(FIRST_REPO_ID, FIRST_REPO_ID + NUM_REPOS))
    repo_org = {repo_id: rng.choice(org_ids) for repo_id in repo_ids}
    return org_ids, repo_ids, repo_org


def build_grants(rng, user_ids, team_ids, org_ids, repo_ids, repo_org):
    subjects = user_ids + team_ids
    resources = org_ids + repo_ids
    grants = []
    seen = set()
    while len(grants) < NUM_GRANTS:
        subject_id = rng.choice(subjects)
        resource_id = rng.choice(resources)
        key = (subject_id, resource_id)
        if key in seen:
            continue  # one grant per subject/resource pair, like a real system
        seen.add(key)
        role = rng.choices(ROLES, weights=ROLE_WEIGHTS)[0]
        grants.append((subject_id, role, resource_id))

    # Deliberate repo-beats-org case: give one subject a low role on an
    # org and a higher one directly on one repo under it. Random grants
    # are independent per pair, so this isn't guaranteed to happen on its
    # own -- and it's the exact case that proves "take the max, repo can

"""Generates the fixture data described in plan.md: 50k users, 4k teams
(nested up to 8 levels, with a few deliberate cycles and a multi-parent
case), 1k orgs, 20k repos, and ~400k grants.

Run: python backend/scripts/generate_fixture.py
Needs DATABASE_URL pointing at an empty database with schema.sql already applied.
"""
import asyncio
import json
import os
import random
from pathlib import Path

import asyncpg

from fixture_graph import (
    add_second_parents,
    attach_remaining_teams,
    build_team_spine,
    plant_cycles,
)

DATABASE_URL = os.environ.get(
    "DATABASE_URL", "postgresql://repo_access:repo_access@localhost:5432/repo_access"
)

SEED = 42
NUM_USERS = 50_000
NUM_TEAMS = 4_000
MAX_TEAM_DEPTH = 8
NUM_ORGS = 1_000
NUM_REPOS = 20_000
NUM_GRANTS = 400_000

ROLES = ["read", "write", "admin", "owner"]
ROLE_WEIGHTS = [0.55, 0.25, 0.15, 0.05]  # most access is read, fewest are owner

FIRST_USER_ID = 1
FIRST_TEAM_ID = FIRST_USER_ID + NUM_USERS
FIRST_ORG_ID = 1
FIRST_REPO_ID = FIRST_ORG_ID + NUM_ORGS


def build_teams(rng):
    team_ids = list(range(FIRST_TEAM_ID, FIRST_TEAM_ID + NUM_TEAMS))
    edges, depth_by_team = build_team_spine(team_ids, MAX_TEAM_DEPTH)
    spine_leaf_id = team_ids[MAX_TEAM_DEPTH - 1]
    edges, depth_by_team = attach_remaining_teams(
        rng, team_ids, edges, depth_by_team, MAX_TEAM_DEPTH
    )
    edges = add_second_parents(rng, team_ids, edges, fraction=0.03)
    edges, cyclic_pairs = plant_cycles(rng, edges, count=3)
    empty_team_id = team_ids[-1]  # deliberately gets no direct members
    return team_ids, edges, spine_leaf_id, cyclic_pairs, empty_team_id


def assign_users_to_teams(rng, user_ids, team_ids, spine_leaf_id):
    """Most users get one team, some get two, a few get none. A handful
    are pinned under the deepest team so there's a real deep-nesting case
    to point the load test / benchmark at, not just a hoped-for one."""
    edges = []
    deep_user_ids = rng.sample(user_ids, 20)
    for user_id in deep_user_ids:
        edges.append((user_id, spine_leaf_id))

    for user_id in user_ids:
        roll = rng.random()
        if roll < 0.02:
            continue  # no team at all
        edges.append((user_id, rng.choice(team_ids)))
        if roll > 0.95:
            edges.append((user_id, rng.choice(team_ids)))  # second team
    return edges, deep_user_ids


def build_resources(rng):
    org_ids = list(range(FIRST_ORG_ID, FIRST_ORG_ID + NUM_ORGS))
    repo_ids = list(range(FIRST_REPO_ID, FIRST_REPO_ID + NUM_REPOS))
    repo_org = {repo_id: rng.choice(org_ids) for repo_id in repo_ids}
    return org_ids, repo_ids, repo_org


def build_grants(rng, user_ids, team_ids, org_ids, repo_ids, repo_org):
    subjects = user_ids + team_ids
    resources = org_ids + repo_ids
    grants = []
    seen = set()
    while len(grants) < NUM_GRANTS:
        subject_id = rng.choice(subjects)
        resource_id = rng.choice(resources)
        key = (subject_id, resource_id)
        if key in seen:
            continue  # one grant per subject/resource pair, like a real system
        seen.add(key)
        role = rng.choices(ROLES, weights=ROLE_WEIGHTS)[0]
        grants.append((subject_id, role, resource_id))

    # Deliberate repo-beats-org case: give one subject a low role on an
    # org and a higher one directly on one repo under it. Random grants
    # are independent per pair, so this isn't guaranteed to happen on its
    # own -- and it's the exact case that proves "take the max, repo can
    # beat org" (see README) actually works.
    override_subject = rng.choice(subjects)
    override_org = rng.choice(org_ids)
    override_repo = rng.choice([r for r, o in repo_org.items() if o == override_org])
    grants.append((override_subject, "read", override_org))
    grants.append((override_subject, "owner", override_repo))
    override_case = {
        "subject_id": override_subject,
        "org_id": override_org,
        "repo_id": override_repo,
        "org_role": "read",
        "repo_role": "owner",
    }
    return grants, override_case


async def main():
    rng = random.Random(SEED)
    conn = await asyncpg.connect(DATABASE_URL)

    user_ids = list(range(FIRST_USER_ID, FIRST_USER_ID + NUM_USERS))
    team_ids, team_edges, spine_leaf_id, cyclic_pairs, empty_team_id = build_teams(rng)
    membership_pool = [t for t in team_ids if t != empty_team_id]
    membership_edges, deep_user_ids = assign_users_to_teams(
        rng, user_ids, membership_pool, spine_leaf_id
    )
    org_ids, repo_ids, repo_org = build_resources(rng)
    grants, override_case = build_grants(rng, user_ids, team_ids, org_ids, repo_ids, repo_org)

    async with conn.transaction():
        await conn.copy_records_to_table(
            "subjects",
            records=[(uid, "user", f"user-{uid}") for uid in user_ids]
            + [(tid, "team", f"team-{tid}") for tid in team_ids],
            columns=["id", "type", "name"],
        )
        await conn.copy_records_to_table(
            "resources",
            records=[(oid, "org", None, f"org-{oid}") for oid in org_ids]
            + [(rid, "repo", repo_org[rid], f"repo-{rid}") for rid in repo_ids],
            columns=["id", "type", "org_id", "name"],
        )
        await conn.copy_records_to_table(
            "team_relationships",
            records=team_edges + membership_edges,
            columns=["subject_id", "belongs_to_team_id"],
        )
        await conn.copy_records_to_table(
            "grants",
            records=grants,
            columns=["subject_id", "role", "resource_id"],
        )
        # We inserted explicit ids above; bump the sequences so the app's
        # own inserts (grants, memberships) don't collide with them later.
        await conn.execute("SELECT setval('subjects_id_seq', (SELECT MAX(id) FROM subjects))")
        await conn.execute("SELECT setval('resources_id_seq', (SELECT MAX(id) FROM resources))")

    manifest = {
        "deep_user_ids": deep_user_ids,
        "spine_leaf_team_id": spine_leaf_id,
        "cyclic_team_pairs": cyclic_pairs,
        "empty_team_id": empty_team_id,
        "repo_beats_org_case": override_case,
    }
    manifest_path = Path(__file__).with_name("fixture_manifest.json")
    manifest_path.write_text(json.dumps(manifest, indent=2))

    await conn.close()
    print(
        f"Inserted {NUM_USERS} users, {NUM_TEAMS} teams, {NUM_ORGS} orgs, "
        f"{NUM_REPOS} repos, {len(grants)} grants."
    )
    print(f"Manifest written to {manifest_path}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

"""Pure graph-building for the team hierarchy fixture. No DB access here on
purpose, so this is easy to read and reason about on its own.
generate_fixture.py calls these and handles the actual database writes.
"""


def build_team_spine(team_ids, depth):
    """First `depth` team ids become a straight chain, root to leaf.

    This guarantees one concrete chain that actually reaches max depth,
    instead of hoping random attachment happens to get there.
    """
    spine = team_ids[:depth]
    edges = [(spine[i], spine[i - 1]) for i in range(1, len(spine))]
    depth_by_team = {team_id: i for i, team_id in enumerate(spine)}
    return edges, depth_by_team


def attach_remaining_teams(rng, team_ids, edges, depth_by_team, max_depth):
    """Every team not already placed gets attached under a random team
    that isn't already at max depth."""
    placed = set(depth_by_team)
    for team_id in team_ids:
        if team_id in placed:
            continue
        eligible = [t for t, d in depth_by_team.items() if d < max_depth - 1]
        parent_id = rng.choice(eligible)
        depth_by_team[team_id] = depth_by_team[parent_id] + 1
        edges.append((team_id, parent_id))
        placed.add(team_id)
    return edges, depth_by_team


def add_second_parents(rng, team_ids, edges, fraction):
    """A handful of teams get a second, independent parent.

    The schema doesn't guarantee one parent per team, so the fixture
    should actually exercise that instead of only ever producing a clean
    tree that hides the case.
    """
    sample_size = int(len(team_ids) * fraction)
    for team_id in rng.sample(team_ids, sample_size):
        other_parent = rng.choice(team_ids)
        if other_parent != team_id:
            edges.append((team_id, other_parent))
    return edges


def plant_cycles(rng, edges, count):
    """Makes a handful of teams cyclic: walks down a few hops from a
    random team and adds an edge back up, so a descendant ends up as its
    own ancestor's parent too.

    R4 expects real cycles to be in the data. Since we write the
    generator ourselves, that only happens if we put them there.
    Returns the new edges plus the (ancestor, descendant) pairs made
    cyclic, so the manifest can record exactly which teams they are.
    """
    children_of = {}
    for child, parent in edges:
        children_of.setdefault(parent, []).append(child)

    planted = []
    candidates = [team for team, kids in children_of.items() if kids]
    for ancestor in rng.sample(candidates, min(count, len(candidates))):
        descendant = ancestor
        for _ in range(rng.randint(2, 5)):
            kids = children_of.get(descendant)
            if not kids:
                break
            descendant = rng.choice(kids)
        if descendant != ancestor:
            edges.append((ancestor, descendant))
            planted.append((ancestor, descendant))
    return edges, planted

"""Generates the fixture data described in plan.md: 50k users, 4k teams
(nested up to 8 levels, with a few deliberate cycles and a multi-parent
case), 1k orgs, 20k repos, and ~400k grants.

Run: python backend/scripts/generate_fixture.py
Needs DATABASE_URL pointing at an empty database with schema.sql already applied.
"""
import asyncio
import json
import os
import random
from pathlib import Path

import asyncpg

from fixture_graph import (
    add_second_parents,
    attach_remaining_teams,
    build_team_spine,
    plant_cycles,
)

DATABASE_URL = os.environ.get(
    "DATABASE_URL", "postgresql://repo_access:repo_access@localhost:5432/repo_access"
)

SEED = 42
NUM_USERS = 50_000
NUM_TEAMS = 4_000
MAX_TEAM_DEPTH = 8
NUM_ORGS = 1_000
NUM_REPOS = 20_000
NUM_GRANTS = 400_000

ROLES = ["read", "write", "admin", "owner"]
ROLE_WEIGHTS = [0.55, 0.25, 0.15, 0.05]  # most access is read, fewest are owner

FIRST_USER_ID = 1
FIRST_TEAM_ID = FIRST_USER_ID + NUM_USERS
FIRST_ORG_ID = 1
FIRST_REPO_ID = FIRST_ORG_ID + NUM_ORGS


def build_teams(rng):
    team_ids = list(range(FIRST_TEAM_ID, FIRST_TEAM_ID + NUM_TEAMS))
    edges, depth_by_team = build_team_spine(team_ids, MAX_TEAM_DEPTH)
    spine_leaf_id = team_ids[MAX_TEAM_DEPTH - 1]
    spine_ids = set(team_ids[:MAX_TEAM_DEPTH])
    edges, depth_by_team = attach_remaining_teams(
        rng, team_ids, edges, depth_by_team, MAX_TEAM_DEPTH
    )
    # Keep the spine itself untouched by extra parents, so it stays exactly
    # 8 levels deep -- one clean, known-depth case to benchmark against.
    # Non-spine teams can still end up deeper than 8 through this (which is
    # the point: the assignment warns not to assume 8 is a hard max).
    non_spine_ids = [t for t in team_ids if t not in spine_ids]
    edges = add_second_parents(rng, non_spine_ids, edges, fraction=0.03)
    edges, cyclic_pairs = plant_cycles(rng, edges, count=3)
    empty_team_id = team_ids[-1]  # deliberately gets no direct members
    return team_ids, edges, spine_leaf_id, cyclic_pairs, empty_team_id


def assign_users_to_teams(rng, user_ids, team_ids, spine_leaf_id):
    """Most users get one team, some get two, a few get none. A handful
    are pinned under the deepest team so there's a real deep-nesting case
    to point the load test / benchmark at, not just a hoped-for one."""
    edges = []
    deep_user_ids = rng.sample(user_ids, 20)
    for user_id in deep_user_ids:
        edges.append((user_id, spine_leaf_id))

    for user_id in user_ids:
        roll = rng.random()
        if roll < 0.02:
            continue  # no team at all
        edges.append((user_id, rng.choice(team_ids)))
        if roll > 0.95:
            edges.append((user_id, rng.choice(team_ids)))  # second team
    return edges, deep_user_ids


def build_resources(rng):
    org_ids = list(range(FIRST_ORG_ID, FIRST_ORG_ID + NUM_ORGS))
    repo_ids = list(range(FIRST_REPO_ID, FIRST_REPO_ID + NUM_REPOS))
    repo_org = {repo_id: rng.choice(org_ids) for repo_id in repo_ids}
    return org_ids, repo_ids, repo_org


def build_grants(rng, user_ids, team_ids, org_ids, repo_ids, repo_org):
    subjects = user_ids + team_ids
    resources = org_ids + repo_ids
    grants = []
    seen = set()
    while len(grants) < NUM_GRANTS:
        subject_id = rng.choice(subjects)
        resource_id = rng.choice(resources)
        key = (subject_id, resource_id)
        if key in seen:
            continue  # one grant per subject/resource pair, like a real system
        seen.add(key)
        role = rng.choices(ROLES, weights=ROLE_WEIGHTS)[0]
        grants.append((subject_id, role, resource_id))

    # Deliberate repo-beats-org case: give one subject a low role on an
    # org and a higher one directly on one repo under it. Random grants
    # are independent per pair, so this isn't guaranteed to happen on its
    # own -- and it's the exact case that proves "take the max, repo can
    # beat org" (see README) actually works.
    override_subject = rng.choice(subjects)
    override_org = rng.choice(org_ids)
    override_repo = rng.choice([r for r, o in repo_org.items() if o == override_org])
    grants.append((override_subject, "read", override_org))
    grants.append((override_subject, "owner", override_repo))
    override_case = {
        "subject_id": override_subject,
        "org_id": override_org,
        "repo_id": override_repo,
        "org_role": "read",
        "repo_role": "owner",
    }
    return grants, override_case


async def main():
    rng = random.Random(SEED)
    conn = await asyncpg.connect(DATABASE_URL)

    user_ids = list(range(FIRST_USER_ID, FIRST_USER_ID + NUM_USERS))
    team_ids, team_edges, spine_leaf_id, cyclic_pairs, empty_team_id = build_teams(rng)
    membership_pool = [t for t in team_ids if t != empty_team_id]
    membership_edges, deep_user_ids = assign_users_to_teams(
        rng, user_ids, membership_pool, spine_leaf_id
    )
    org_ids, repo_ids, repo_org = build_resources(rng)
    grants, override_case = build_grants(rng, user_ids, team_ids, org_ids, repo_ids, repo_org)

    async with conn.transaction():
        await conn.copy_records_to_table(
            "subjects",
            records=[(uid, "user", f"user-{uid}") for uid in user_ids]
            + [(tid, "team", f"team-{tid}") for tid in team_ids],
            columns=["id", "type", "name"],
        )
        await conn.copy_records_to_table(
            "resources",
            records=[(oid, "org", None, f"org-{oid}") for oid in org_ids]
            + [(rid, "repo", repo_org[rid], f"repo-{rid}") for rid in repo_ids],
            columns=["id", "type", "org_id", "name"],
        )
        await conn.copy_records_to_table(
            "team_relationships",
            records=team_edges + membership_edges,
            columns=["subject_id", "belongs_to_team_id"],
        )
        await conn.copy_records_to_table(
            "grants",
            records=grants,
            columns=["subject_id", "role", "resource_id"],
        )
        # We inserted explicit ids above; bump the sequences so the app's
        # own inserts (grants, memberships) don't collide with them later.
        await conn.execute("SELECT setval('subjects_id_seq', (SELECT MAX(id) FROM subjects))")
        await conn.execute("SELECT setval('resources_id_seq', (SELECT MAX(id) FROM resources))")

    manifest = {
        "deep_user_ids": deep_user_ids,
        "spine_leaf_team_id": spine_leaf_id,
        "cyclic_team_pairs": cyclic_pairs,
        "empty_team_id": empty_team_id,
        "repo_beats_org_case": override_case,
    }
    manifest_path = Path(__file__).with_name("fixture_manifest.json")
    manifest_path.write_text(json.dumps(manifest, indent=2))

    await conn.close()
    print(
        f"Inserted {NUM_USERS} users, {NUM_TEAMS} teams, {NUM_ORGS} orgs, "
        f"{NUM_REPOS} repos, {len(grants)} grants."
    )
    print(f"Manifest written to {manifest_path}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

"""Generates the fixture data described in plan.md: 50k users, 4k teams
(nested up to 8 levels, with a few deliberate cycles and a multi-parent
case), 1k orgs, 20k repos, and ~400k grants.

Run: python backend/scripts/generate_fixture.py
Needs DATABASE_URL pointing at an empty database with schema.sql already applied.
"""
import asyncio
import json
import os
import random
from pathlib import Path

import asyncpg

from fixture_graph import (
    add_second_parents,
    attach_remaining_teams,
    build_team_spine,
    plant_cycles,
)

DATABASE_URL = os.environ.get(
    "DATABASE_URL", "postgresql://repo_access:repo_access@localhost:5432/repo_access"
)

SEED = 42
NUM_USERS = 50_000
NUM_TEAMS = 4_000
MAX_TEAM_DEPTH = 8
NUM_ORGS = 1_000
NUM_REPOS = 20_000
NUM_GRANTS = 400_000

ROLES = ["read", "write", "admin", "owner"]
ROLE_WEIGHTS = [0.55, 0.25, 0.15, 0.05]  # most access is read, fewest are owner

FIRST_USER_ID = 1
FIRST_TEAM_ID = FIRST_USER_ID + NUM_USERS
FIRST_ORG_ID = 1
FIRST_REPO_ID = FIRST_ORG_ID + NUM_ORGS


def build_teams(rng):
    team_ids = list(range(FIRST_TEAM_ID, FIRST_TEAM_ID + NUM_TEAMS))
    edges, depth_by_team = build_team_spine(team_ids, MAX_TEAM_DEPTH)
    spine_leaf_id = team_ids[MAX_TEAM_DEPTH - 1]
    spine_ids = set(team_ids[:MAX_TEAM_DEPTH])
    edges, depth_by_team = attach_remaining_teams(
        rng, team_ids, edges, depth_by_team, MAX_TEAM_DEPTH
    )
    # Keep the spine itself untouched by extra parents, so it stays exactly
    # 8 levels deep -- one clean, known-depth case to benchmark against.
    # Non-spine teams can still end up deeper than 8 through this (which is
    # the point: the assignment warns not to assume 8 is a hard max).
    non_spine_ids = [t for t in team_ids if t not in spine_ids]
    edges = add_second_parents(rng, non_spine_ids, edges, fraction=0.03)
    edges, cyclic_pairs = plant_cycles(rng, edges, count=3, exclude=spine_ids)
    empty_team_id = team_ids[-1]  # deliberately gets no direct members
    return team_ids, edges, spine_leaf_id, cyclic_pairs, empty_team_id


def assign_users_to_teams(rng, user_ids, team_ids, spine_leaf_id):
    """Most users get one team, some get two, a few get none. A handful
    are pinned under the deepest team so there's a real deep-nesting case
    to point the load test / benchmark at, not just a hoped-for one."""
    edges = []
    deep_user_ids = rng.sample(user_ids, 20)
    for user_id in deep_user_ids:
        edges.append((user_id, spine_leaf_id))

    for user_id in user_ids:
        roll = rng.random()
        if roll < 0.02:
            continue  # no team at all
        edges.append((user_id, rng.choice(team_ids)))
        if roll > 0.95:
            edges.append((user_id, rng.choice(team_ids)))  # second team
    return edges, deep_user_ids


def build_resources(rng):
    org_ids = list(range(FIRST_ORG_ID, FIRST_ORG_ID + NUM_ORGS))
    repo_ids = list(range(FIRST_REPO_ID, FIRST_REPO_ID + NUM_REPOS))
    repo_org = {repo_id: rng.choice(org_ids) for repo_id in repo_ids}
    return org_ids, repo_ids, repo_org


def build_grants(rng, user_ids, team_ids, org_ids, repo_ids, repo_org):
    subjects = user_ids + team_ids
    resources = org_ids + repo_ids
    grants = []
    seen = set()
    while len(grants) < NUM_GRANTS:
        subject_id = rng.choice(subjects)
        resource_id = rng.choice(resources)
        key = (subject_id, resource_id)
        if key in seen:
            continue  # one grant per subject/resource pair, like a real system
        seen.add(key)
        role = rng.choices(ROLES, weights=ROLE_WEIGHTS)[0]
        grants.append((subject_id, role, resource_id))

    # Deliberate repo-beats-org case: give one subject a low role on an
    # org and a higher one directly on one repo under it. Random grants
    # are independent per pair, so this isn't guaranteed to happen on its
    # own -- and it's the exact case that proves "take the max, repo can
    # beat org" (see README) actually works.
    override_subject = rng.choice(subjects)
    override_org = rng.choice(org_ids)
    override_repo = rng.choice([r for r, o in repo_org.items() if o == override_org])
    grants.append((override_subject, "read", override_org))
    grants.append((override_subject, "owner", override_repo))
    override_case = {
        "subject_id": override_subject,
        "org_id": override_org,
        "repo_id": override_repo,
        "org_role": "read",
        "repo_role": "owner",
    }
    return grants, override_case


async def main():
    rng = random.Random(SEED)
    conn = await asyncpg.connect(DATABASE_URL)

    user_ids = list(range(FIRST_USER_ID, FIRST_USER_ID + NUM_USERS))
    team_ids, team_edges, spine_leaf_id, cyclic_pairs, empty_team_id = build_teams(rng)
    membership_pool = [t for t in team_ids if t != empty_team_id]
    membership_edges, deep_user_ids = assign_users_to_teams(
        rng, user_ids, membership_pool, spine_leaf_id
    )
    org_ids, repo_ids, repo_org = build_resources(rng)
    grants, override_case = build_grants(rng, user_ids, team_ids, org_ids, repo_ids, repo_org)

    async with conn.transaction():
        await conn.copy_records_to_table(
            "subjects",
            records=[(uid, "user", f"user-{uid}") for uid in user_ids]
            + [(tid, "team", f"team-{tid}") for tid in team_ids],
            columns=["id", "type", "name"],
        )
        await conn.copy_records_to_table(
            "resources",
            records=[(oid, "org", None, f"org-{oid}") for oid in org_ids]
            + [(rid, "repo", repo_org[rid], f"repo-{rid}") for rid in repo_ids],
            columns=["id", "type", "org_id", "name"],
        )
        await conn.copy_records_to_table(
            "team_relationships",
            records=team_edges + membership_edges,
            columns=["subject_id", "belongs_to_team_id"],
        )
        await conn.copy_records_to_table(
            "grants",
            records=grants,
            columns=["subject_id", "role", "resource_id"],
        )
        # We inserted explicit ids above; bump the sequences so the app's
        # own inserts (grants, memberships) don't collide with them later.
        await conn.execute("SELECT setval('subjects_id_seq', (SELECT MAX(id) FROM subjects))")
        await conn.execute("SELECT setval('resources_id_seq', (SELECT MAX(id) FROM resources))")

    manifest = {
        "deep_user_ids": deep_user_ids,
        "spine_leaf_team_id": spine_leaf_id,
        "cyclic_team_pairs": cyclic_pairs,
        "empty_team_id": empty_team_id,
        "repo_beats_org_case": override_case,
    }
    manifest_path = Path(__file__).with_name("fixture_manifest.json")
    manifest_path.write_text(json.dumps(manifest, indent=2))

    await conn.close()
    print(
        f"Inserted {NUM_USERS} users, {NUM_TEAMS} teams, {NUM_ORGS} orgs, "
        f"{NUM_REPOS} repos, {len(grants)} grants."
    )
    print(f"Manifest written to {manifest_path}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

content.text:
**Checkbox done: `backend/scripts/generate_fixture.py` + `fixture_graph.py`**

What's built:
- `backend/scripts/fixture_graph.py` — pure functions building the team hierarchy: a guaranteed 8-level spine, random attachment for the rest, multi-parent edges, planted cycles. No DB code, so it's easy to read on its own.
- `backend/scripts/generate_fixture.py` — orchestrates it, bulk-inserts into Postgres via `asyncpg`, writes `fixture_manifest.json` recording exactly which ids are the deep-nesting case, the cyclic teams, the empty team, and the repo-beats-org case.
- `backend/requirements.txt` — just `asyncpg` for now (the Postgres driver, needed given we're using Postgres + async — flagging since it's a new dependency, even though a minimal/necessary one).
- `.gitignore` added (pycache, venvs, node_modules, .env) — hadn't been created yet.

**One real bug I caught and fixed while testing, not just eyeballing:** the first version's "clean depth-8 case" actually measured at depth 14, because the multi-parent injection sampled from *all* teams including the deliberate spine, and the "deep users" also got extra random team memberships from the general assignment loop. Both would have muddied the one clean benchmark case R1's p95 measurement needs. Fixed by excluding the spine from multi-parent/cycle injection and excluding deep users from the general per-user loop. Verified the fix with actual recursive SQL queries against the container, not just re-reading the code.

**How to test it yourself:**
```bash
docker compose up -d postgres
cd backend/scripts
pip install -r ../requirements.txt   # or use a venv
DATABASE_URL="postgresql://repo_access:repo_access@localhost:5432/repo_access" python generate_fixture.py
cat fixture_manifest.json
```
Then sanity-check counts and the deep chain, e.g.:
```bash
psql -h localhost -p 5432 -U repo_access -d repo_access -c "SELECT count(*) FROM grants;"
```
You should see 50000 users, 4000 teams, 1000 orgs, 20000 repos, ~400002 grants.

Let me know if this looks good — once approved I'll commit and move to `cache.py`.

import unittest

from app import cache


class TestCache(unittest.TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        cache.invalidate_all()

    def test_miss_returns_none(self):
        self.assertIsNone(cache.get(1))

    def test_set_then_get_returns_the_same_team_set(self):
        cache.set(1, {10, 20, 30})
        team_ids, cached_at = cache.get(1)
        self.assertEqual(team_ids, {10, 20, 30})
        self.assertIsNotNone(cached_at)

    def test_invalidate_user_clears_only_that_user(self):
        cache.set(1, {10})
        cache.set(2, {20})
        cache.invalidate_user(1)
        self.assertIsNone(cache.get(1))
        self.assertIsNotNone(cache.get(2))

    def test_invalidate_user_on_absent_user_is_a_no_op(self):
        cache.invalidate_user(999)  # should not raise

    def test_invalidate_all_clears_everyone(self):
        cache.set(1, {10})
        cache.set(2, {20})
        cache.invalidate_all()
        self.assertIsNone(cache.get(1))
        self.assertIsNone(cache.get(2))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main()

"""The fast path: R1 (check) lives here. explain() (R3) comes later and
deliberately does not reuse get_team_set's cache -- see README.
"""
from app import cache, db
from app.models import Role

# Walks team_relationships upward from a user, collecting every team
# reachable (direct or nested). The visited array stops it looping on a
# cycle -- the fixture has some on purpose, see plan.md.
_ANCESTOR_TEAMS_SQL = """
WITH RECURSIVE ancestors(team_id, visited) AS (
    SELECT belongs_to_team_id, ARRAY[belongs_to_team_id]
    FROM team_relationships
    WHERE subject_id = $1 AND belongs_to_team_id IS NOT NULL
  UNION ALL
    SELECT tr.belongs_to_team_id, a.visited || tr.belongs_to_team_id
    FROM team_relationships tr
    JOIN ancestors a ON tr.subject_id = a.team_id
    WHERE tr.belongs_to_team_id IS NOT NULL
      AND NOT (tr.belongs_to_team_id = ANY(a.visited))
)
SELECT DISTINCT team_id FROM ancestors
"""

# A grant counts if it's on the repo itself or on the repo's org -- an org
# grant covers its repos, but a repo-level grant can still be higher (see
# README's "Org grants cover their repos, but don't cap them").
_ROLE_LOOKUP_SQL = """
SELECT g.role
FROM grants g
JOIN resources r ON r.id = $2
WHERE g.subject_id = ANY($1::bigint[])
  AND g.resource_id IN ($2, r.org_id)
"""


async def get_team_set(user_id: int) -> set[int]:
    cached = cache.get(user_id)
    if cached is not None:
        team_ids, _cached_at = cached
        return team_ids

    pool = await db.get_pool()
    rows = await pool.fetch(_ANCESTOR_TEAMS_SQL, user_id)
    team_ids = {row["team_id"] for row in rows}
    cache.set(user_id, team_ids)
    return team_ids


async def resolve_role(subject_ids: set[int], repo_id: int) -> Role | None:
    pool = await db.get_pool()
    rows = await pool.fetch(_ROLE_LOOKUP_SQL, list(subject_ids), repo_id)
    roles = [Role.from_str(row["role"]) for row in rows]
    return max(roles) if roles else None


async def check(user_id: int, action: Role, repo_id: int) -> bool:
    team_ids = await get_team_set(user_id)
    role = await resolve_role({user_id} | team_ids, repo_id)
    return role is not None and role >= action
